FileBrowser reverse-proxy bypass: direct external access to exposed port 8085 AIDelivery Medium
Hunts inbound connections that reach the FileBrowser container port (published as 8085 via Docker -p 8085:80) directly from a public/untrusted source, bypassing the reverse proxy (nginx/Traefik/Caddy) that is the sole security boundary for auth.method=proxy. Because auth/proxy.go has zero origin validation, any client that can reach the port directly can forge the X-Remote-User header, so a direct external hit on the exposed port is the network pre-condition for CVE-2026-54089 exploitation. Rationale: Article states exploitation requires an attacker who 'can reach the server directly' and cites Docker '-p 8085:80' publishing to 0.0.0.0; a direct public hit on 8085 is the network pre-condition for the header-forgery bypass. Cross-checked against the GHSA advisory and the auth/proxy.go root-cause writeup. Cross-checked against: • https://github.com/advisories/GHSA-xqp3-jq6g-x3qm • https://advisories.gitlab.com/golang/github.com/filebrowser/filebrowser/v2/CVE-2026-54089/ • https://cvereports.com/reports/CVE-2026-54089
ATT&CKT1190 T1199
Data sourcesNetwork_Traffic.All_Traffic
Expected false positives · estimated rate: medium — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Internet-wide scanners (Shodan/Censys/Palo Alto Expanse) probing the exposed port
  • External uptime/health-check monitors (Pingdom, UptimeRobot) hitting the port for availability
  • A sysadmin intentionally reaching the port directly for debugging as described in the article
  • Cloud load-balancer or NAT gateway health probes that appear as public IPs
  • Security team's own external attack-surface scans
Response runbook
1) Triage: confirm the FileBrowser instance runs auth.method=proxy and that 8085 is meant to be proxy-only; identify the reverse-proxy egress IP set and check whether SourceIP is outside it. 2) Contain: firewall/security-group the container port to the reverse proxy IP only (bind 127.0.0.1 or restrict inbound), and rotate the JWT signing key to invalidate any minted tokens. 3) Hunt: pull FileBrowser/WAF logs for /api/login requests from the same SourceIP carrying an X-Remote-User header and for any user accounts created in the last 30 days (auto-creation primitive).
DeviceNetworkEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(7d)
| where ActionType == "InboundConnectionAccepted"
| where LocalPort == 8085                       // FileBrowser container port from -p 8085:80
| where RemoteIPType == "Public"
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, RemoteIP, RemotePort, LocalIP, LocalPort, InitiatingProcessFileName
| order by Timestamp desc
CommonSecurityLog
| where TimeGenerated > ago(7d)
| where DestinationPort == 8085                  // FileBrowser exposed container port
| where DeviceAction in~ ("allow","permit","accept","allowed")
| where ipv4_is_private(SourceIP) == false
| project TimeGenerated, DeviceVendor, DeviceProduct, SourceIP, DestinationIP, DestinationPort, DeviceAction, RequestURL
| order by TimeGenerated desc

FileBrowser proxy-auth header forgery naming admin on /api/login AIExploitation High
Hunts POST /api/login requests carrying a proxy-auth identity header (X-Remote-User / X-Forwarded-User / X-Authenticated-User / X-Auth) whose value names an administrative account (admin/administrator/root) while originating from outside the trusted reverse-proxy egress range. Because ProxyAuth.Auth() trusts the header with no origin/secret check, a forged admin header from a non-proxy source is the direct signature of the CVE-2026-54089 authentication bypass and full admin takeover. Rationale: Uses the exact attack primitive from the PoC: a forged X-Remote-User (configurable via auth.header; ecosystem defaults are X-Remote-User / X-Forwarded-User per FileBrowser docs) naming 'admin' sent to /api/login. Header value + non-proxy source IP is high-fidelity because legitimate proxy traffic always originates from the proxy egress IP and the proxy sets the header itself. Defender/Falcon/CloudWatch blank: HTTP request headers are not present in EDR or CloudTrail telemetry — this needs a WAF/proxy that logs request headers. Cross-checked against GHSA advisory, auth/proxy.go lines 21-28, and filebrowser.org/authentication.html. Cross-checked against: • https://github.com/advisories/GHSA-xqp3-jq6g-x3qm • https://advisories.gitlab.com/golang/github.com/filebrowser/filebrowser/v2/CVE-2026-54089/ • https://filebrowser.org/authentication.html
ATT&CKT1548 T1556 T1078
Data sourcesWeb.Web
Expected false positives · estimated rate: low — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • A misconfigured second reverse proxy not in the known egress allowlist forwarding legitimate SSO traffic
  • Penetration testers / red team validating the CVE from an internal-but-non-proxy host
  • A legitimate admin whose real username is literally 'admin' logging in through a newly-added proxy node
  • WAF logging the header on blocked (not forwarded) requests during tuning
  • Automated config-management tooling hitting /api/login with a service header
Suppression filter
| where tolower(ProxyUser) in ("admin","administrator","root") and ipv4_is_private(SourceIP) == false
Response runbook
1) Triage: confirm the SourceIP is not a sanctioned reverse-proxy egress IP; if it is not, treat as a live bypass — a valid admin JWT was almost certainly minted. 2) Contain: block the SourceIP at the perimeter, restrict the FileBrowser port to proxy-only, rotate the JWT signing secret to revoke issued tokens, and force re-auth. 3) Hunt: enumerate all FileBrowser user accounts (auto-creation may have added attacker-named users), review /api/settings and /api/users changes and any file download/exec activity from the same session, and audit for non-admin X-Remote-User values from the same source.
CommonSecurityLog
| where TimeGenerated > ago(7d)
| where RequestURL has "/api/login"
| where RequestContext has_any ("X-Remote-User", "X-Forwarded-User", "X-Authenticated-User", "X-WebAuth-User", "REMOTE_USER", "X-Auth-User")   // proxy-auth identity header
| extend ProxyUser = extract(@"(?i)(?:X-Remote-User|X-Forwarded-User|X-Authenticated-User|X-WebAuth-User|REMOTE_USER|X-Auth-User)\s*[:=]\s*([^\s;,]+)", 1, RequestContext)
| where tolower(ProxyUser) in ("admin","administrator","root")     // privileged username in forged header
| where ipv4_is_private(SourceIP) == false                          // not from trusted proxy egress
| project TimeGenerated, DeviceVendor, DeviceProduct, SourceIP, DestinationIP, RequestMethod, RequestURL, ProxyUser
| order by TimeGenerated desc

FileBrowser auto-account-creation: first-seen username in proxy auth header AIInstallation Medium
Correlates /api/login requests carrying a proxy-auth username header from an untrusted source against a 30-day baseline of previously-seen usernames, surfacing brand-new (first-seen) usernames. FileBrowser's createUser() unconditionally provisions a real account when the header names a non-existent user, giving attackers a no-authorization account-creation primitive; a first-seen username submitted from a non-proxy IP is the signature of backdoor account provisioning. Rationale: Targets the article's second primitive: 'specifying a non-existent username causes the server to automatically create a new user account.' A first-seen X-Remote-User value from a non-proxy IP maps directly to createUser() being triggered by an attacker-controlled header. Leftanti-join against a 30-day baseline expresses first-seen without ML. Defender/Falcon/CloudWatch blank: request-header username is only visible in WAF/proxy logs, not EDR/CloudTrail. Cross-checked against: • https://github.com/advisories/GHSA-xqp3-jq6g-x3qm • https://advisories.gitlab.com/golang/github.com/filebrowser/filebrowser/v2/CVE-2026-54089/
ATT&CKT1136.001 T1098
Data sourcesWeb.Web
Expected false positives · estimated rate: medium — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Genuine onboarding of a new employee whose SSO username is passed for the first time through a proxy node not yet in the trusted list
  • A newly-provisioned reverse proxy whose egress IP has not been added to the private/allowlist ranges
  • Baseline gap: usernames legitimately used before the 30-day window appearing 'first-seen'
  • Service accounts or automation logging in via a header for the first time after a config change
  • WAF header-parsing quirks that extract a truncated username value
Suppression filter
| where ProxyUser !in~ ("guest","anonymous","health","healthcheck","monitor","probe")
Response runbook
1) Triage: list current FileBrowser accounts and compare against the first-seen ProxyUser value; a matching newly-created account confirms the auto-creation primitive fired. 2) Contain: delete the attacker-provisioned account(s), restrict the port to proxy-only, and rotate the JWT signing secret. 3) Hunt: review whether the new account's default permissions include execute/create/modify (article notes Defaults.Apply may grant these), inspect file operations and command execution tied to that username, and search for additional first-seen usernames from the same SourceIP.
let Baseline = CommonSecurityLog
    | where TimeGenerated between (ago(30d) .. ago(1d))
    | where RequestURL has "/api/login"
    | extend ProxyUser = extract(@"(?i)(?:X-Remote-User|X-Forwarded-User|X-Authenticated-User|X-WebAuth-User|REMOTE_USER|X-Auth-User)\s*[:=]\s*([^\s;,]+)", 1, RequestContext)
    | where isnotempty(ProxyUser)
    | summarize by tolower(ProxyUser);
CommonSecurityLog
| where TimeGenerated > ago(1d)
| where RequestURL has "/api/login"
| extend ProxyUser = extract(@"(?i)(?:X-Remote-User|X-Forwarded-User|X-Authenticated-User|X-WebAuth-User|REMOTE_USER|X-Auth-User)\s*[:=]\s*([^\s;,]+)", 1, RequestContext)
| where isnotempty(ProxyUser)
| extend ProxyUser = tolower(ProxyUser)

FileBrowser post-bypass admin API actions (DELETE/PUT /api/users, /api/settings) AIActions on Objectives Medium
Hunts privileged FileBrowser REST API calls — DELETE/PUT/POST against /api/users, /api/settings and /api/resources — originating from outside the trusted reverse-proxy egress range. After forging an admin JWT via the header bypass, an attacker uses these admin endpoints to modify settings, create/delete users, and manipulate files; admin-verb API traffic from a non-proxy source is the post-compromise action signature of CVE-2026-54089. Rationale: Maps to the article's outcome: a minted admin JWT (perm.admin:true) grants full control, and the PoC shows admin API calls such as GET /api/settings. This UC widens to the state-changing admin verbs an attacker would issue post-bypass. Source-IP restriction to non-proxy origins keeps fidelity. Header-level context isn't required, so this is expressible on standard proxy/webserver access logs. Cross-checked against: • https://github.com/advisories/GHSA-xqp3-jq6g-x3qm • https://advisories.gitlab.com/golang/github.com/filebrowser/filebrowser/v2/CVE-2026-54089/
ATT&CKT1548 T1078
Data sourcesWeb.Web
Expected false positives · estimated rate: medium — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Legitimate admin performing settings/user management through a proxy node not in the allowlist
  • Automated backup/config tooling issuing PUT /api/settings on a schedule
  • A monitoring integration polling /api/resources
  • Red-team/pentest validation of the CVE
  • New reverse-proxy egress IP not yet added to the private/allowlist ranges
Response runbook
1) Triage: confirm SourceIP is non-proxy; correlate to any preceding /api/login with an X-Remote-User admin header from the same IP to confirm the bypass chain. 2) Contain: block the SourceIP, restrict the port to proxy-only, rotate the JWT signing secret, and snapshot current FileBrowser settings/users for forensics. 3) Hunt: diff /api/settings and user list against last-known-good, review file resource operations (downloads/deletes) from the session, and check for command execution if the compromised/created account has the execute permission.
CommonSecurityLog
| where TimeGenerated > ago(7d)
| where RequestMethod in~ ("DELETE","PUT","POST")
| where RequestURL has_any ("/api/users", "/api/settings", "/api/resources")
| where ipv4_is_private(SourceIP) == false                 // not from trusted proxy egress
| project TimeGenerated, DeviceVendor, DeviceProduct, SourceIP, DestinationIP, RequestMethod, RequestURL
| order by TimeGenerated desc

FileBrowser identity-cycling: 3+ user identities from one untrusted source in 5 min AIExploitation High
Flags a single non-proxy source IP presenting 3 or more distinct FileBrowser user identities to the API within a 5-minute window. Legitimate proxy traffic carries one authenticated identity per user and the proxy egress IP is stable per session; rapid identity-switching from one direct source indicates the attacker is cycling forged X-Remote-User header values to impersonate multiple accounts — the 'impersonate any user' behaviour of CVE-2026-54089. Rationale: Directly implements the article's 'impersonate any user' claim: because the header is attacker-chosen with no verification, an attacker enumerating/impersonating accounts produces many distinct identities from a single direct source in a short window — a shape legitimate per-user proxy auth cannot produce. dcount over a 5-minute bin is a threshold+temporal correlation, so Sigma is skipped. Defender/Falcon/CloudWatch blank: the authenticated username per web request lives in proxy/WAF logs, not EDR or CloudTrail. Cross-checked against: • https://github.com/advisories/GHSA-xqp3-jq6g-x3qm • https://cvereports.com/reports/CVE-2026-54089
ATT&CKT1078 T1550.001
Data sourcesWeb.Web
Expected false positives · estimated rate: low — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Multiple real users behind a single corporate NAT / CGNAT egress IP hitting FileBrowser (if that egress isn't classified as proxy)
  • A VPN concentrator or shared jump host from which several admins legitimately work
  • Automated test suites iterating multiple test users against the API
  • A load/perf test cycling synthetic accounts
  • Mobile users sharing a carrier-grade NAT address
Response runbook
1) Triage: inspect the Users set from the flagged SrcIpAddr — presence of admin/root alongside several unrelated usernames strongly indicates impersonation cycling; confirm the IP is not a sanctioned NAT/proxy egress. 2) Contain: block the SourceIP, restrict the FileBrowser port to proxy-only, and rotate the JWT signing secret to void all forged tokens. 3) Hunt: for each impersonated username, review file downloads/deletes and settings/user changes in the same window, and check whether any of those identities were auto-created (never existed before).
ImWebSession
| where TimeGenerated > ago(1d)
| where Url has "/api/"
| where isnotempty(SrcUsername)
| where ipv4_is_private(SrcIpAddr) == false
| summarize DistinctUsers = dcount(SrcUsername), Users = make_set(SrcUsername, 20), Requests = count()
          by SrcIpAddr, bin(TimeGenerated, 5m)
| where DistinctUsers >= 3          // 3+ identities from one non-proxy IP in 5 min = header cycling, not legit multi-user
| order by DistinctUsers desc
CLOUD
Toggle if your env has no CIM data-model acceleration.
| tstats summariesonly=true dc(Web.user) as distinct_users, values(Web.user) as users, count from datamodel=Web.Web where Web.url="*/api/*" Web.src_category!=proxy by _time span=5m, Web.src, Web.dest | `drop_dm_object_name(Web)` | where distinct_users >= 3 | sort - distinct_users
| tstats summariesonly=false dc(Web.user) as distinct_users, values(Web.user) as users, count from datamodel=Web.Web where Web.url="*/api/*" Web.src_category!=proxy by _time span=5m, Web.src, Web.dest | `drop_dm_object_name(Web)` | where distinct_users >= 3 | sort - distinct_users
FileBrowser instance configured with auth.method=proxy (exploitable-config exposure) AIReconnaissance Medium
Surfaces FileBrowser processes started with proxy authentication enabled (auth.method=proxy plus an auth.header such as X-Remote-User), which is the precondition that makes CVE-2026-54089 exploitable. This is a proactive exposure hunt on endpoint process telemetry to inventory at-risk hosts before, or independently of, any live exploitation — pair the results with the direct-external-access UC to prioritise instances that are both proxy-auth and network-exposed. Rationale: Article states the vuln is 'NOT exploitable on default configuration' and requires auth.method=proxy with an auth.header (default X-Remote-User); inventorying processes launched with these flags directly enumerates exploitable hosts. Uses the exact config tokens (auth.method, auth.header, X-Remote-User) and the filebrowser binary name. Defender/Falcon/ImProcessCreate are viable because this is host process telemetry, not HTTP. CloudWatch blank: not AWS-native. NOTE flags the coverage gap for env-var/config-file deployments where flags aren't on the command line. Cross-checked against: • https://github.com/advisories/GHSA-xqp3-jq6g-x3qm • https://filebrowser.org/authentication.html • https://advisories.gitlab.com/golang/github.com/filebrowser/filebrowser/v2/CVE-2026-54089/
ATT&CKT1190 T1592.001
Data sourcesEndpoint.Processes
Expected false positives · estimated rate: medium — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • A correctly-hardened instance bound to 127.0.0.1 behind a proxy that strips client headers (proxy-auth enabled but not exploitable)
  • Non-production/test FileBrowser instances intentionally running proxy auth
  • A container image rebuild re-launching the same safe config repeatedly
  • Config-management (Ansible/Helm) restarts re-emitting the same flags
  • Legacy proxy-auth deployment already firewalled at the network layer
Response runbook
1) Triage: for each flagged host, determine the listen bind address (127.0.0.1 vs 0.0.0.0) and whether the port is reachable from untrusted networks — correlate with the direct-external-access UC. 2) Contain: for exposed instances, restrict the port to the reverse-proxy egress only and configure the proxy to strip/overwrite the identity header on inbound client requests. 3) Hunt: on confirmed-exposed hosts, pull proxy/WAF logs for /api/login requests carrying X-Remote-User from non-proxy sources and audit the FileBrowser user list for accounts created via the auto-creation primitive.
DeviceProcessEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(30d)
| where FileName has "filebrowser"
| where ProcessCommandLine has "proxy"
      and (ProcessCommandLine has "auth.method" or ProcessCommandLine has "--auth.header" or ProcessCommandLine has "X-Remote-User")
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, AccountName, FileName, FolderPath, ProcessCommandLine
| order by Timestamp desc
// NOTE: only catches flag-based config; env-var (FB_AUTH_METHOD) or config.json/DB config will not appear in cmdline
ImProcessCreate
| where TimeGenerated > ago(30d)
| where TargetProcessName has "filebrowser"
| where TargetProcessCommandLine has "proxy"
      and (TargetProcessCommandLine has "auth.method" or TargetProcessCommandLine has "auth.header" or TargetProcessCommandLine has "X-Remote-User")
| project TimeGenerated, DvcHostname, ActorUsername, TargetProcessName, TargetProcessCommandLine
| order by TimeGenerated desc

Actions on Objectives
Detected
Reconnaissance. Attacker researches the target — OSINT, scanning, enumeration. → [LLM] SiYuan kernel config (conf.json) written — audit for empty/missing AccessAuthCode · Asset exposure — vulnerability matches article CVE(s)
Weaponization. Coupling exploit code with deliverable payload (e.g. weaponized PDF/Office doc, trojanized installer).
Delivery. Transmitting the weapon (phishing email, USB, watering hole, drive-by, malicious ad).
Exploitation. Triggering the exploit — vulnerability/macro/trust abuse to execute code. → [LLM] External browser process connects to SiYuan kernel loopback admin port 127.0.0.1:6806 · Trusted vendor binary / installer launching unusual children
Installation. Establishing persistence on the host — backdoor, service, scheduled task, registry key. → [LLM] Browser extension manifest rewritten adding networking/host permissions (supply-chain) · Suspicious browser extension installation

Actions on Objectives. Lateral movement, credential dumping, data theft, ransomware, sabotage. → Infostealer — non-browser process accessing browser cookie/login DBs
External browser process connects to SiYuan kernel loopback admin port 127.0.0.1:6806 AIExploitation Medium
Hunts a Chrome/Chromium/Edge browser process opening a loopback connection to the SiYuan Note kernel HTTP server on port 6806. Per CVE-2026-54069 the kernel blanket-trusts any `chrome-extension://` Origin as RoleAdministrator, so a browser-context connection to 6806 (as opposed to the Electron siyuan.exe app itself) is the in-flight exploitation signal for a malicious/compromised extension exfiltrating notes or injecting stored XSS. Rationale: Uses the article's exact kernel bind address (127.0.0.1) and port (6806) plus the browser-process constraint that distinguishes a rogue extension from SiYuan's own Electron siyuan.exe process — the Origin header itself (chrome-extension://) is not carried in EDR/network telemetry so the browser-to-loopback 5-tuple is the highest-fidelity observable proxy for it. Loopback capture varies by EDR agent, hence hunting tier; Sentinel ImNetworkSession lacks process attribution so triage the host manually. Cross-checked against: • https://github.com/advisories/GHSA-hvr9-72v2-fff3
ATT&CKT1176 T1078
Data sourcesNetwork_Traffic.All_Traffic
Expected false positives · estimated rate: medium — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Official SiYuan web-clipper browser extension legitimately posting captures to the kernel on 6806
  • Developer or power-user testing the SiYuan API from a browser devtools/console session
  • Browser-based localhost tooling reusing port 6806
  • SiYuan run in browser (non-desktop) mode where the UI itself is a browser tab talking to 6806
Response runbook
1) Triage: identify the exact browser process (InitiatingProcessId/CommandLine) and enumerate that user's installed extensions; confirm whether the official SiYuan web-clipper is installed and expected on this host. 2) Contain: if no sanctioned SiYuan clipper is installed, disable/remove the browser's recently-updated extensions and, if a note workspace holds sensitive data, set a non-empty AccessAuthCode in SiYuan and restart the kernel. 3) Hunt: pivot on the same host/user for subsequent connections to attacker infrastructure (stored-XSS callback like attacker.example/steal) and for conf.json writes indicating /api/system/setConf tampering.
DeviceNetworkEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(7d)
| where RemotePort == 6806
| where RemoteIP in ("127.0.0.1", "::1")
| where InitiatingProcessFileName in~ ("chrome.exe","msedge.exe","brave.exe","chromium.exe","opera.exe","vivaldi.exe")
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, InitiatingProcessAccountName, InitiatingProcessFileName, InitiatingProcessId, InitiatingProcessCommandLine, RemoteIP, RemotePort, LocalPort
| order by Timestamp desc
ImNetworkSession
| where TimeGenerated > ago(7d)
| where DstPortNumber == 6806
| where DstIpAddr in ("127.0.0.1", "::1")
| project TimeGenerated, DvcHostname, SrcIpAddr, SrcUsername, DstIpAddr, DstPortNumber, NetworkApplicationProtocol, Url, DvcAction
| order by TimeGenerated desc

SiYuan kernel config (conf.json) written — audit for empty/missing AccessAuthCode AIReconnaissance Low
Config-audit hunt that surfaces writes to a SiYuan workspace conf.json so an analyst can verify the AccessAuthCode field. CVE-2026-54069 is trivially exploitable on desktop installs where AccessAuthCode defaults to an empty string, so any host running SiYuan with unset auth is exposed to unauthenticated admin API access from any browser extension. Rationale: Anchors on the article's stated config surface — conf.json holding the AccessAuthCode that defaults empty on ContainerStd desktop installs. EDR file telemetry cannot read the field's value, so this is an inventory/audit pivot: every hit is a host to check manually for unset auth, hence Low confidence and hunting tier. Cross-checked against: • https://github.com/advisories/GHSA-hvr9-72v2-fff3
ATT&CKT1078.001
Data sourcesEndpoint.Filesystem
Expected false positives · estimated rate: high — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Routine SiYuan settings changes writing conf.json during normal use
  • SiYuan data-sync/backup clients copying the workspace including conf.json
  • First-run workspace initialization creating conf.json
  • Users legitimately editing SiYuan preferences
Response runbook
1) Triage: on each returned host, open the referenced conf.json and inspect the AccessAuthCode value — empty string, null, or missing = exposed. 2) Contain: for exposed hosts holding sensitive notes, direct the owner to set a strong AccessAuthCode and upgrade SiYuan past the fixed kernel version (>= 0.0.0-20260628153353-2d5d72223df4). 3) Hunt: on any host confirmed exposed, review for browser-to-127.0.0.1:6806 connections (UC1) and outbound connections to unfamiliar domains indicating prior data exfiltration via /api/query/sql.
DeviceFileEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(30d)
| where FileName =~ "conf.json"
| where FolderPath has "siyuan"
| where ActionType in ("FileCreated","FileModified")
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, FolderPath, FileName, ActionType, InitiatingProcessAccountName, InitiatingProcessFileName, InitiatingProcessFolderPath
| order by Timestamp desc
ImFileEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(30d)
| where TargetFileName =~ "conf.json"
| where TargetFilePath has "siyuan"
| project TimeGenerated, DvcHostname, ActorUsername, TargetFilePath, TargetFileName, EventType, ActingProcessName, ActingProcessCommandLine
| order by TimeGenerated desc

Browser extension manifest rewritten adding networking/host permissions (supply-chain) AIInstallation Low
Hunts writes to Chrome/Edge/Brave extension manifest.json or the profile Preferences/Secure Preferences files — the artifacts rewritten when an installed extension is updated with new permissions. CVE-2026-54069 is amplified by a supply-chain model where a previously-benign extension pushes a malicious update; because localhost:6806 is reachable with zero declared host_permissions, watch specifically for extension permission/manifest churn preceding the loopback abuse in UC1. Rationale: Grounded in the article's supply-chain amplification note ('a single compromised popular Chrome extension update can silently exploit every SiYuan desktop user') and the fact that the PoC extension needs zero host_permissions — so any manifest/permission churn on a Chromium profile is the earliest artifact of a weaponized update. High FP because browsers legitimately update extensions; best used chained with UC1 (same host, followed by a 6806 loopback connection). Sentinel path uses ImFileEvent (not the Defender-only DeviceRegistryEvents) to stay schema-valid. Cross-checked against: • https://github.com/advisories/GHSA-hvr9-72v2-fff3
ATT&CKT1176
Data sourcesEndpoint.Filesystem
Expected false positives · estimated rate: high — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Chrome/Edge silently auto-updating installed extensions in the background
  • User manually installing or updating a browser extension
  • Enterprise force-installed (ExtensionInstallForcelist) extension deployment
  • New browser profile creation writing fresh Preferences/manifest files
  • Browser sync reconciling extension state across devices
Response runbook
1) Triage: identify which extension ID's manifest changed and diff old vs new permissions (look for newly added networking, <all_urls>, or host permissions); check the extension's reputation and update timestamp. 2) Contain: if the extension is unsanctioned or the update is unexpected, disable/remove it via browser management policy across affected hosts. 3) Hunt: on the same host/user, correlate within a short window for a browser connection to 127.0.0.1:6806 (UC1) and for outbound C2/exfil connections, confirming the update was weaponized against a running SiYuan kernel.
DeviceFileEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(7d)
| where FileName in~ ("manifest.json","Secure Preferences","Preferences")
| where FolderPath has_any (@"\Google\Chrome\User Data\", @"\Microsoft\Edge\User Data\", @"\BraveSoftware\", @"\Chromium\User Data\")
| where InitiatingProcessFileName in~ ("chrome.exe","msedge.exe","brave.exe","chromium.exe")
| where ActionType in ("FileCreated","FileModified")
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, InitiatingProcessAccountName, FolderPath, FileName, ActionType, InitiatingProcessFileName
| order by Timestamp desc
ImFileEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(7d)
| where TargetFileName in~ ("manifest.json","Secure Preferences","Preferences")
| where TargetFilePath has_any (@"\Google\Chrome\User Data\", @"\Microsoft\Edge\User Data\", @"\BraveSoftware\", @"\Chromium\User Data\")
| where ActingProcessName has_any ("chrome.exe","msedge.exe","brave.exe","chromium.exe")
| project TimeGenerated, DvcHostname, ActorUsername, TargetFilePath, TargetFileName, EventType, ActingProcessName
| order by TimeGenerated desc

Authorizer /authorize implicit-flow token leak to off-origin redirect_uri (CVE-2026-54072) AIExploitation High
Hunts exploitation of CVE-2026-54072: /authorize requests using response_type=token or id_token whose redirect_uri points at a host different from the Authorizer server, causing access_token/id_token/refresh_token to be appended to a 302 redirect toward an attacker-controlled URL. Rationale: Keys on the exact vulnerable route (/authorize), the exact implicit-flow trigger values (response_type=token / id_token), and the redirect_uri host != server host mismatch that is the CWE-601 root cause. Cross-checked GHSA-h29v-hj44-q8cv, the GitLab advisory, and sibling GHSA-x3f4-v83f-7wp2. Cross-checked against: • https://github.com/advisories/GHSA-h29v-hj44-q8cv • https://advisories.gitlab.com/golang/github.com/authorizerdev/authorizer/CVE-2026-54072/ • https://github.com/advisories/GHSA-x3f4-v83f-7wp2
ATT&CKT1190 T1528
Data sourcesWeb.Web
Expected false positives · estimated rate: low — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Legitimate SPA OAuth client registered with an implicit-flow callback on a partner/CDN domain distinct from the Authorizer host
  • Internal test/staging automation exercising the implicit flow across environment hostnames
  • Mobile app custom-scheme callbacks that regex-parse as a different host
  • A reverse proxy rewriting Host header so ServerHost != registered origin
  • DAST scanners probing the OAuth endpoint
Suppression filter
| where tolower(RedirectHost) != tolower(HttpHostName) and RedirectHost !in~ ("partner-callback.example.com", "login.mycdn.example.com")
Response runbook
1) Triage: url-decode redirect_uri per hit; confirm the host is external/attacker-controlled and response_type is token/id_token with a 302 response. 2) Contain: confirm Authorizer >= 0.0.0-20260409051328-bd3f5baf6d3d; else add AllowedOrigins/WAF enforcement on /authorize and revoke refresh tokens for victims. 3) Hunt: review /userinfo and downstream API calls under stolen bearer tokens; pivot the off-origin host across oauth_login, verify_email, magic_link_login, forgot_password.
ImWebSession
| where TimeGenerated > ago(7d)
| where Url has "/authorize"
| where Url matches regex @"(?i)response_type(=|%3D)(id_)?token"
| extend RedirectRaw = extract(@"(?i)redirect_uri(?:=|%3D)([^&]+)", 1, Url)
| where isnotempty(RedirectRaw)
| extend RedirectDecoded = url_decode(RedirectRaw)
| extend RedirectHost = extract(@"(?i)https?://([^/:?]+)", 1, RedirectDecoded)
| where isnotempty(RedirectHost) and tolower(RedirectHost) != tolower(HttpHostName)
| project TimeGenerated, SrcIpAddr, ServerHost = HttpHostName, RedirectHost, HttpMethod, HttpStatusCode, Url
| order by TimeGenerated desc
title: Authorizer OAuth2 implicit-flow token leak via off-origin redirect_uri (CVE-2026-54072)

description: Detects /authorize requests using implicit-flow response_type=token or id_token combined with an off-origin redirect_uri, the exploitation shape of CVE-2026-54072 in authorizerdev/authorizer.

  - https://advisories.gitlab.com/golang/github.com/authorizerdev/authorizer/CVE-2026-54072/

Authorizer unauthenticated /graphql client_id reconnaissance (CVE-2026-54072 pre-exploit) AIReconnaissance Medium
Hunts the recon step of CVE-2026-54072 where an unauthenticated attacker queries public /graphql with {meta{client_id}} to harvest the client_id needed for the malicious /authorize link. Surfaces meta/client_id introspection and single-source /graphql bursts. Rationale: Uses the article's Step-1 recon primitive ({meta{client_id}} against /graphql). POST bodies aren't in access logs, so it catches the GET-introspection variant directly and flags single-source burst volume as a proxy for the POST sweep. Cross-checked against: • https://github.com/advisories/GHSA-h29v-hj44-q8cv
ATT&CKT1592.004 T1190
Data sourcesWeb.Web
Expected false positives · estimated rate: medium — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Authorizer's own front-end calling /graphql for meta/client_id on page load from CDN egress IPs
  • GraphQL IDE / schema-introspection developer tools
  • Uptime/health monitors polling /graphql
  • API gateway aggregating many users behind one IP inflating the burst
  • POST-based real recon is invisible (body not logged) and will be missed
Response runbook
1) Triage: confirm introspection hits carried no Authorization header/cookie and returned 200; for bursts, distinguish known front-end/CDN egress from unfamiliar IP/ASN. 2) Contain: block unauthorized source IP/ASN at WAF, treat client_id as public, prioritise patching /authorize. 3) Hunt: correlate recon source/time with subsequent /authorize implicit-flow (UC1) and the sibling handlers oauth_login/verify_email/magic_link_login/forgot_password.
ImWebSession
| where TimeGenerated > ago(7d)
| where Url has "/graphql"
| extend GetIntrospection = iff(Url has "meta" and Url has "client_id", 1, 0)
| summarize Requests=count(), IntrospectionHits=sum(GetIntrospection), Statuses=make_set(HttpStatusCode,5), Methods=make_set(HttpMethod,3), FirstSeen=min(TimeGenerated), LastSeen=max(TimeGenerated) by SrcIpAddr, ServerHost = HttpHostName
| where IntrospectionHits > 0 or Requests >= 20
| order by IntrospectionHits desc, Requests desc

Authorizer /authorize redirect_uri iteration — multiple distinct targets from one source AIExploitation Medium
Detects an attacker iterating CVE-2026-54072 by issuing /authorize requests with 3+ distinct redirect_uri hosts from one source IP within 5 minutes — probing which attacker-controlled domain succeeds. Legit clients use a fixed callback host. Rationale: Article notes the attacker may try multiple attacker-controlled domains/subdomains. Distinct redirect_uri hosts per source per 5-minute bucket vs the fixed-callback baseline cleanly isolates iteration/probing. Cross-checked against: • https://github.com/advisories/GHSA-h29v-hj44-q8cv
ATT&CKT1190 T1528
Data sourcesWeb.Web
Expected false positives · estimated rate: medium — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Multi-tenant/white-label deployment where one gateway drives OAuth for several apps each with its own callback host
  • QA/DAST fuzzing redirect_uri across environments
  • CDN/NAT egress IP aggregating many users
  • Load-testing tooling parameterising callback URLs
  • Browser prefetch/redirect chains generating host variants
Response runbook
1) Triage: inspect RedirectHosts for the source — probing shows unrelated/new domains, legit multi-tenant shows known app domains; confirm response_type=token present. 2) Contain: WAF-block the source IP; if any host is malicious, revoke tokens for affected accounts and deny-list it. 3) Hunt: pivot each RedirectHost to victims 302'd with tokens (UC1); check DNS/TI on domains; see if the source did /graphql recon (UC2) first.
ImWebSession
| where TimeGenerated > ago(7d)
| where Url has "/authorize"
| extend RedirectRaw = extract(@"(?i)redirect_uri(?:=|%3D)([^&]+)", 1, Url)
| where isnotempty(RedirectRaw)
| extend RedirectHost = extract(@"(?i)https?://([^/:?]+)", 1, url_decode(RedirectRaw))
| where isnotempty(RedirectHost)
| summarize DistinctRedirectHosts=dcount(RedirectHost), RedirectHosts=make_set(RedirectHost,15), AuthorizeRequests=count() by SrcIpAddr, bin(TimeGenerated, 5m)
| where DistinctRedirectHosts >= 3
| order by DistinctRedirectHosts desc

| eval redirect_decoded=urldecode(redirect_raw)
| rex field=redirect_decoded "(?i)https?://(?<redirect_host>[^/:?]+)"

Spike in Authorizer /authorize 302 redirects to off-origin hosts (bulk token exfiltration) AIActions on Objectives Medium
Volume-anomaly detection for mass exploitation of CVE-2026-54072: a statistically significant spike in /authorize 302 responses redirecting to a redirect_uri host different from the Authorizer server, catching bulk token exfiltration. Rationale: Reviewer-requested volume complement: baselines /authorize 302s to off-origin redirect_uri hosts hourly and alerts on >3-sigma AND >5x spikes, catching scaled exploitation. Uses the article's exact 302 status and redirect-host-mismatch root cause. Cross-checked against: • https://github.com/advisories/GHSA-h29v-hj44-q8cv
ATT&CKT1190 T1528
Data sourcesWeb.Web
Expected false positives · estimated rate: medium — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • New legitimate OAuth client onboarded with a cross-domain callback causing a step-change in off-origin 302 volume
  • Marketing/SSO campaign driving a login burst through a partner callback host
  • Proxy Host-header rewriting making same-origin callbacks appear off-origin
  • Sparse baseline (low-traffic tenant) tripping the multiplier on any small burst
  • At-scale load tests or synthetic OAuth monitors
Response runbook
1) Triage: break down the anomalous hour by RedirectHost and SrcIp — one dominant host = exploitation; spread across known partner domains = benign onboarding. 2) Contain: WAF-block the destination hosts and source IPs, confirm patch >= 0.0.0-20260409051328-bd3f5baf6d3d, mass-revoke refresh tokens for accounts in the window. 3) Hunt: enumerate accounts 302'd to the malicious host and review /userinfo + downstream API usage; check recon (UC2) and iteration (UC3) from the same infrastructure.
ImWebSession
| where TimeGenerated > ago(14d)
| where Url has "/authorize" and tostring(HttpStatusCode) == "302"
| extend RedirectRaw = extract(@"(?i)redirect_uri(?:=|%3D)([^&]+)", 1, Url)
| where isnotempty(RedirectRaw)
| extend RedirectHost = extract(@"(?i)https?://([^/:?]+)", 1, url_decode(RedirectRaw))
| where isnotempty(RedirectHost) and tolower(RedirectHost) != tolower(HttpHostName)
| make-series OffOrigin302 = count() default=0 on TimeGenerated from ago(14d) to now() step 1h by ServerHost = HttpHostName
| extend (anomalies, score, baseline) = series_decompose_anomalies(OffOrigin302, 3.0)
| mv-expand TimeGenerated to typeof(datetime), OffOrigin302 to typeof(long), anomalies to typeof(long), baseline to typeof(double)
| where anomalies == 1 and OffOrigin302 > 5 * baseline
| project TimeGenerated, ServerHost, OffOrigin302, baseline, score
| order by TimeGenerated desc

Reconnaissance. Attacker researches the target — OSINT, scanning, enumeration. → Asset exposure — vulnerability matches article CVE(s)

Delivery. Transmitting the weapon (phishing email, USB, watering hole, drive-by, malicious ad). → [LLM] Non-SiYuan process writing synced snippet store data\snippets\conf.json

Actions on Objectives. Lateral movement, credential dumping, data theft, ransomware, sabotage.
SiYuan Electron renderer (nodeIntegration) spawning shell/LOLBin child — XSS-to-RCE AIExploitation High
Hunts the RCE stage of CVE-2026-54067 (and the sibling SiYuan XSS-to-RCE bugs): a stored snippet/caption/README breaks out of its HTML context and, because the renderer runs with nodeIntegration:true, calls require('child_process') to spawn a command interpreter. A Markdown note app should essentially never parent cmd.exe/powershell.exe, so this parent->child pair is high-fidelity across the whole SiYuan RCE bug class. Rationale: Anchored on InitiatingProcessFileName=siyuan.exe (the Electron main/renderer binary confirmed in the advisory as running nodeIntegration:true/contextIsolation:false) parenting a command interpreter — the observable end state of require('child_process').execSync from injected JS. Node's execSync on Windows spawns cmd.exe, making cmd.exe the highest-value child. Robust across all SiYuan XSS-to-RCE variants. Cross-checked against: • https://github.com/siyuan-note/siyuan/security/advisories/GHSA-phhp-9rm9-6gr2 • https://advisories.gitlab.com/golang/github.com/siyuan-note/siyuan/kernel/CVE-2026-44670/ • https://cve.threatint.eu/CVE/CVE-2026-54067
ATT&CKT1203 T1059.003 T1059.001
Data sourcesEndpoint.Processes
Expected false positives · estimated rate: low — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • SiYuan document export to PDF/Word invoking a bundled pandoc/wkhtmltopdf helper (verify child binary is the export helper, not a shell)
  • User-configured 'open with' / external-command plugins in SiYuan that legitimately shell out
  • A power-user snippet the owner wrote themselves that intentionally calls a benign command (confirm with the user)
  • SiYuan auto-update or crash-reporter helper launched via cmd.exe wrapper
Suppression filter
| where not (ChildCmd has_any ("pandoc", "wkhtmltopdf", "--export", "SiYuan-Kernel"))
Response runbook
1) TRIAGE: Pull the child ProcessCommandLine and SHA256 — a benign export helper looks nothing like a shell one-liner. Check whether the same user recently edited a CSS/JS snippet or synced a workspace. 2) CONTAIN: Isolate the host, kill the child process tree, and revoke/rotate any SiYuan Cloud / S3 / WebDAV sync credentials for that workspace so the poisoned snippet can't re-propagate. 3) HUNT: Retrieve data/snippets/conf.json from every peer that syncs the same workspace and grep for '</style>' or 'onerror='; upgrade all SiYuan clients to >=3.7.0; sweep other hosts for siyuan.exe parenting interpreters over the last 30 days.
DeviceProcessEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(7d)
| where InitiatingProcessFileName =~ "siyuan.exe"
| where FileName in~ ("cmd.exe","powershell.exe","pwsh.exe","wscript.exe","cscript.exe","mshta.exe","rundll32.exe","regsvr32.exe","curl.exe","certutil.exe","bitsadmin.exe","calc.exe")
| where AccountName !endswith "$"
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, AccountName, ParentImage = InitiatingProcessFolderPath, ParentCmd = InitiatingProcessCommandLine, ChildImage = FolderPath, ChildCmd = ProcessCommandLine, SHA256
| order by Timestamp desc
SecurityEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(7d)
| where EventID == 4688
| where ParentProcessName endswith "\\siyuan.exe"
| where NewProcessName has_any ("\\cmd.exe","\\powershell.exe","\\pwsh.exe","\\wscript.exe","\\cscript.exe","\\mshta.exe","\\rundll32.exe","\\regsvr32.exe","\\curl.exe","\\certutil.exe","\\bitsadmin.exe","\\calc.exe")
| where not(SubjectUserName endswith "$")
| project TimeGenerated, Computer, SubjectUserName, ParentProcessName, NewProcessName, CommandLine
| order by TimeGenerated desc
title: SiYuan Electron Renderer Spawning Command Interpreter (XSS-to-RCE)
id: 6a1f2c7e-9b4d-4e2a-8c3f-1d7b0e5a4c92
description: Detects the SiYuan Electron desktop app (nodeIntegration:true) spawning a shell or LOLBin child process, the RCE stage of CVE-2026-54067 and sibling stored-XSS-to-RCE bugs.
references:

  - https://github.com/siyuan-note/siyuan/security/advisories/GHSA-phhp-9rm9-6gr2
author: SOC Detection Engineering
date: 2026/07/10
tags:

  - attack.t1059.003
  - attack.t1059.001
logsource:
  category: process_creation
  product: windows
detection:
  selection:
    ParentImage|endswith: '\siyuan.exe'
    Image|endswith:
      - '\cmd.exe'
      - '\powershell.exe'
      - '\pwsh.exe'
      - '\wscript.exe'
      - '\cscript.exe'
      - '\mshta.exe'

  condition: selection
level: high
source:windows.sysmon @EventID:1 @ParentImage:(*\\siyuan.exe OR *\\SiYuan.exe) @Image:(*\\cmd.exe OR *\\Cmd.exe OR *\\powershell.exe OR *\\PowerShell.exe OR *\\pwsh.exe OR *\\mshta.exe OR *\\MSHTA.EXE OR *\\wscript.exe OR *\\cscript.exe OR *\\rundll32.exe OR *\\RegSvr32.exe OR *\\regsvr32.exe OR *\\curl.exe OR *\\certutil.exe OR *\\bitsadmin.exe)
#event_simpleName=ProcessRollup2 ParentBaseFileName=/siyuan\.exe/i
| ImageFileName=/\\(cmd|powershell|pwsh|mshta|wscript|cscript|rundll32|regsvr32|curl|certutil|bitsadmin|calc)\.exe$/i
| groupBy([aid, ComputerName, ParentBaseFileName, ImageFileName, CommandLine], function=count())
ENDPOINT
Toggle if your env has no CIM data-model acceleration.
| tstats `summariesonly` count min(_time) as firstTime max(_time) as lastTime from datamodel=Endpoint.Processes where Processes.parent_process_name="siyuan.exe" AND Processes.process_name IN ("cmd.exe","powershell.exe","pwsh.exe","wscript.exe","cscript.exe","mshta.exe","rundll32.exe","regsvr32.exe","curl.exe","certutil.exe","bitsadmin.exe","calc.exe","conhost.exe") by Processes.dest Processes.user Processes.parent_process Processes.parent_process_name Processes.process Processes.process_name Processes.process_id | `drop_dm_object_name(Processes)` | convert ctime(firstTime) ctime(lastTime) | sort - lastTime
| tstats summariesonly=false count min(_time) as firstTime max(_time) as lastTime from datamodel=Endpoint.Processes where Processes.parent_process_name="siyuan.exe" AND Processes.process_name IN ("cmd.exe","powershell.exe","pwsh.exe","wscript.exe","cscript.exe","mshta.exe","rundll32.exe","regsvr32.exe","curl.exe","certutil.exe","bitsadmin.exe","calc.exe","conhost.exe") by Processes.dest Processes.user Processes.parent_process Processes.parent_process_name Processes.process Processes.process_name Processes.process_id | `drop_dm_object_name(Processes)` | convert ctime(firstTime) ctime(lastTime) | sort - lastTime
Non-SiYuan process writing synced snippet store data\snippets\conf.json AIDelivery Medium
Hunts the plant/delivery stage of CVE-2026-54067: the malicious CSS snippet is stored in the workspace file data/snippets/conf.json, which syncs to every peer. When a process OTHER than the SiYuan kernel writes that file — e.g. a Dropbox/Syncthing/Google Drive sync client, a text editor, or a shared-drive process — it indicates the snippet store was tampered with out-of-band, exactly the 'workspace-write compromise via shared filesystem' vector the advisory calls out. Rationale: Uses the exact storage path from the advisory (data/snippets/conf.json, referenced at kernel/model/repository.go:1748,1798) and excludes the legitimate writer (the SiYuan kernel). A write by a sync client or editor is the out-of-band tamper path the advisory enumerates (Dropbox/Syncthing/network share/git). Cross-checked against: • https://cve.threatint.eu/CVE/CVE-2026-54067 • https://advisories.gitlab.com/golang/github.com/siyuan-note/siyuan/kernel/CVE-2026-44670/
ATT&CKT1080 T1195
Data sourcesEndpoint.Filesystem
Expected false positives · estimated rate: medium — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Dropbox.exe / SyncthingTray.exe / googledrivefs.exe legitimately syncing a workspace whose owner edited snippets on another device (benign but the exact tamper vector — inspect the resulting content)
  • A backup agent (Veeam, Duplicati, Acronis) reading/rewriting the workspace folder
  • User editing conf.json directly in VS Code / Notepad++ during troubleshooting
  • Git client (git.exe) pulling a workspace tracked in version control
  • Antivirus/EDR quarantine-and-restore touching the file
Suppression filter
| where InitiatingProcessFileName !in~ ("veeam.backup.shell.exe","duplicati.exe","backup.exe") and InitiatingProcessFileName !endswith "git.exe"
Response runbook
1) TRIAGE: Open the written data/snippets/conf.json and grep for '</style>', 'onerror=', '<img', or 'child_process' — a benign sync writes normal CSS/JS. Note the writing process and account. 2) CONTAIN: If payload strings are present, quarantine the workspace, block sync (pause Dropbox/Syncthing, revoke WebDAV/S3 creds), and prevent SiYuan from loading the poisoned snippet until cleaned. 3) HUNT: Enumerate every device syncing the same workspace and check for the same conf.json write; pivot to UC #1 (siyuan.exe spawning a shell) on those hosts to see if RCE already fired; confirm all clients are >=3.7.0.
DeviceFileEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(30d)
| where FolderPath has @"\data\snippets\" and FileName =~ "conf.json"
| where ActionType in ("FileCreated","FileModified","FileRenamed")
| where InitiatingProcessFileName !in~ ("siyuan.exe","siyuan-kernel.exe","kernel.exe")
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, InitiatingProcessAccountName, InitiatingProcessFileName, InitiatingProcessFolderPath, InitiatingProcessCommandLine, FolderPath, FileName, ActionType
| order by Timestamp desc
ImFileEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(30d)
| where TargetFilePath has @"\data\snippets\" and TargetFileName =~ "conf.json"
| where EventType in ("FileCreated","FileModified","FileRenamed")
| where not(ActingProcessName has "siyuan")
| project TimeGenerated, DvcHostname, ActorUsername, ActingProcessName, ActingProcessCommandLine, TargetFilePath, EventType
| order by TimeGenerated desc

YesWiki Bazar CalcField eval() RCE — dangerous PHP functions in form-save request AIExploitation Medium
Hunts inbound web requests to a YesWiki server carrying PHP execution primitives (system(), passthru(), shell_exec(), proc_open(), file_get_contents()) in the Bazar Calc-field formula — the CVE-2026-52778 regex-bypass-to-eval() vector. Article-specific because it targets the exact eval() sink and the RCE payload shape shown in the advisory (`abs(1) + system('id')`). Rationale: Anchors on the exact eval() abuse from the advisory (`system('id')` in a Bazar formula) by matching PHP command-execution functions plus a following literal or URL-encoded '(' in the request. Cross-checked GitLab Advisory Database and CVEReports which confirm unauthenticated RCE via CalcField.php formatValuesBeforeSave(). Cross-checked against: • https://advisories.gitlab.com/composer/yeswiki/yeswiki/CVE-2026-52778/ • https://cvereports.com/reports/CVE-2026-52778 • https://github.com/YesWiki/yeswiki/commit/dd2bd8fb099de0d21504bda8a810693b3fcb8e52
ATT&CKT1059.004 T1190
Data sourcesWeb.All_Traffic
Expected false positives · estimated rate: medium — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • A different application on the same WAF legitimately passing text like 'exec(' in a code-snippet or documentation field
  • Security scanners (Nuclei/Burp) probing the site during authorized pentests
  • Developers pasting PHP snippets into a wiki page body
  • WAF already blocking the request (still logs the payload) — treat as blocked-but-attempted, not compromise
Suppression filter
| where DeviceAction != "blocked" and DeviceAction != "deny"
Response runbook
1) Triage: confirm the target host is a YesWiki instance and check its version — if < 4.6.6 it is vulnerable. Pull the full request (body + source IP) and check WAF DeviceAction (blocked vs allowed). 2) Contain: if allowed and host is <4.6.6, block the source IP at the WAF and take the app offline or WAF-virtual-patch the Bazar save endpoint; prioritize upgrading to 4.6.6+. 3) Hunt: pivot to endpoint telemetry on the web host for php-fpm/apache spawning shells (UC3), new .php files under webroot (UC4), and reads of wakka.config.php/.env (UC5) around the request time.
// Point at the WAF/reverse-proxy in front of the YesWiki host. CommonSecurityLog carries the full RequestURL and, on most WAFs, the inspected body in Message/RequestContext.
let Lookback = 7d;
CommonSecurityLog
| where TimeGenerated > ago(Lookback)
| where RequestURL matches regex @"(?i)(system|passthru|shell_exec|proc_open|popen|exec|assert|file_get_contents|base64_decode|phpinfo)\s*(\(|%28)"
    or Message matches regex @"(?i)(system|passthru|shell_exec|proc_open|popen|file_get_contents)\s*(\(|%28)"
| summarize FirstSeen=min(TimeGenerated), LastSeen=max(TimeGenerated), Hits=count(), Sample=any(RequestURL)
          by SourceIP, DestinationHostName, RequestMethod, RequestClientApplication, DeviceProduct
| order by LastSeen desc

YesWiki CalcField ReDoS/stack-overflow DoS — deeply nested parentheses payload AIActions on Objectives Medium
Hunts requests to a YesWiki server containing 8+ consecutive open parentheses (literal or URL-encoded), the CVE-2026-52778 ReDoS/PCRE-stack-overflow vector that crashes the PHP-FPM/Apache worker. Article-specific: matches the advisory's exact DoS PoC of thousands of nested parens against the recursive `(?1)+` regex. Rationale: The advisory's DoS PoC is literally thousands of nested '(' chars; 8+ consecutive open-parens (raw or %28-encoded) never occurs in a genuine math formula, making this a low-FP, high-specificity match on the exact ReDoS payload. Cross-checked against: • https://advisories.gitlab.com/composer/yeswiki/yeswiki/CVE-2026-52778/ • https://cvereports.com/reports/CVE-2026-52778
ATT&CKT1499.004 T1190
Data sourcesWeb.All_Traffic
Expected false positives · estimated rate: low — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • A wiki page body legitimately containing ASCII art or deeply nested code being saved through the same host
  • Automated fuzzing/scanning during an authorized assessment
  • A poorly written legitimate math formula (rare — still worth investigating given the CVE)
  • Copy-pasted Lisp/Scheme code into a wiki field
Response runbook
1) Triage: confirm host is YesWiki <4.6.6; check whether the corresponding PHP-FPM/Apache worker crashed (segfault in dmesg/apache error_log) near the request time and whether availability dropped. 2) Contain: block the source IP, and add a WAF rule rejecting requests with >6 consecutive '(' to the Bazar save endpoint; schedule the 4.6.6 upgrade which replaces the regex+eval with an AST parser. 3) Hunt: check for repeated bursts from the same source (sustained DoS) and correlate with server-health/CPU alerts and 5xx spikes.
// Deeply nested parentheses = the ReDoS/PCRE stack-overflow payload for CalcField.php. 8 chosen as a floor well above any legitimate math formula.
let Lookback = 7d;
CommonSecurityLog
| where TimeGenerated > ago(Lookback)
| where RequestURL matches regex @"(\(){8,}" or RequestURL matches regex @"(%28){8,}"
    or Message matches regex @"(\(){8,}" or Message matches regex @"(%28){8,}"
| summarize FirstSeen=min(TimeGenerated), LastSeen=max(TimeGenerated), Hits=count(), Sample=any(RequestURL)
          by SourceIP, DestinationHostName, RequestMethod, RequestClientApplication
| order by Hits desc

YesWiki post-RCE — php-fpm/apache spawns Unix shell or recon binary (www-data) AIInstallation High
Detects a YesWiki web-server process (php-fpm, apache2/httpd, nginx) spawning a shell or reconnaissance binary — the observable outcome of a successful CalcField eval() RCE running as www-data. This is the strongest, lowest-FP pivot because web daemons almost never legitimately fork sh/id/whoami/curl. Rationale: A web daemon (php-fpm/apache) forking a shell or id/whoami is the canonical outcome of the article's `system('id')` RCE example and is near-zero in normal operation. Parent restricted to YesWiki web-server binaries keeps FP low. Cross-checked against: • https://advisories.gitlab.com/composer/yeswiki/yeswiki/CVE-2026-52778/ • https://github.com/YesWiki/yeswiki/security/advisories/GHSA-px5m-h76g-p7p8
ATT&CKT1059.004 T1190
Data sourcesEndpoint.Processes
Expected false positives · estimated rate: low — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Legitimate YesWiki/plugin features that shell out (e.g. thumbnail generation via ImageMagick 'convert' — not in this binary list, but custom plugins may)
  • Server monitoring/health-check scripts invoked by the web user
  • Deployment or cron tasks briefly running under the www-data account
  • A sysadmin debugging PHP with a manual `php` CLI that itself calls a shell
Suppression filter
| where ProcessCommandLine !has "convert" and ProcessCommandLine !has "healthcheck"
Response runbook
1) Triage: inspect the child ProcessCommandLine — `id`/`whoami`/`uname` strongly indicate hands-on RCE validation; capture the parent php-fpm cmdline and the acting user. 2) Contain: isolate the host, kill the offending process tree, and preserve the apache/php-fpm access logs mapping the request that triggered it. 3) Hunt: look for follow-on webshell writes (UC4), config/credential reads (UC5), outbound C2 from the web user, and new cron/systemd persistence created by www-data.
let Lookback = 7d;
DeviceProcessEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(Lookback)
| where InitiatingProcessFileName matches regex @"(?i)^(php-fpm|php-cgi|php|httpd|apache2|nginx)"
| where FileName in~ ("sh","bash","dash","id","whoami","uname","curl","wget","python","python3","perl","nc","ncat")
| where AccountName !endswith "$"
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, AccountName, InitiatingProcessFileName, InitiatingProcessCommandLine, FileName, ProcessCommandLine, FolderPath, SHA256
| order by Timestamp desc
let Lookback = 7d;
ImProcessCreate
| where TimeGenerated > ago(Lookback)
| where ParentProcessName matches regex @"(?i)(php-fpm|php-cgi|/php$|httpd|apache2|nginx)"
| where ActingProcessName matches regex @"(?i)/(sh|bash|dash|id|whoami|uname|curl|wget|python[0-9.]*|perl|nc|ncat)$"
| project TimeGenerated, DvcHostname, ActorUsername, ParentProcessName, ParentProcessCommandLine, ActingProcessName, ActingProcessCommandLine
| order by TimeGenerated desc

YesWiki webshell drop — web-server process writes new .php file into webroot AIInstallation High
Detects a YesWiki web-server process (php-fpm/apache/nginx) creating a new .php file under the application tree (tools/, bazar/, files/, cache/, custom/) — the persistence step after CalcField eval() RCE. Web servers writing executable PHP is highly abnormal and article-relevant (advisory notes attackers 'inject backdoors' as www-data). Rationale: The advisory explicitly warns attackers can 'inject backdoors' as the web user; a php-fpm/apache process creating a .php file under tools/bazar/files/cache/custom is a direct, high-fidelity webshell-persistence signal specific to the YesWiki webroot layout. Cross-checked against: • https://github.com/advisories/GHSA-px5m-h76g-p7p8 • https://github.com/YesWiki/yeswiki/commit/dd2bd8fb099de0d21504bda8a810693b3fcb8e52
ATT&CKT1505.003 T1105
Data sourcesEndpoint.Filesystem
Expected false positives · estimated rate: low — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Legitimate YesWiki updates/plugin installs performed through the web UI that write .php into custom/ or tools/
  • A YesWiki caching mechanism that materializes compiled .php templates into cache/
  • Composer/deployment running as the web user during a maintenance window
  • Theme or extension imports via the admin console
Suppression filter
| where not (InitiatingProcessCommandLine has_any ("composer","update","install") and FolderPath has "/cache/")
Response runbook
1) Triage: retrieve and read the newly written .php file — look for eval/base64_decode/system/`$_POST`/`$_GET` webshell markers; note the writing process cmdline and user. 2) Contain: quarantine the file, isolate the host, and snapshot for forensics; block the source IP identified from correlated web logs. 3) Hunt: enumerate all recently modified .php files under the webroot, check for the same content hash on other hosts, and review web logs for subsequent requests to the dropped file path.

YesWiki credential access — web user reads wakka.config.php / .env / /etc/passwd AIActions on Objectives Medium
Detects the YesWiki web user (via php-fpm/apache-spawned shell) reading YesWiki's canonical secrets file wakka.config.php, a .env, or /etc/passwd/shadow using cat/grep/curl/base64 — the confidentiality-impact step the advisory calls out (reading '/etc/passwd, .env configuration files'). Product-specific because wakka.config.php holds the YesWiki DB credentials. Rationale: wakka.config.php is YesWiki's canonical config holding DB credentials; combined with the advisory's stated targets (/etc/passwd, .env) and a web-server-spawned reader binary, this captures the exact confidentiality-impact behavior for this CVE. Cross-checked against: • https://github.com/advisories/GHSA-px5m-h76g-p7p8 • https://cvereports.com/reports/CVE-2026-52778
ATT&CKT1552.001 T1005
Data sourcesEndpoint.Processes
Expected false positives · estimated rate: medium — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Legitimate admin or deployment scripts running as the web user that cat/grep wakka.config.php during troubleshooting
  • Backup jobs reading .env / config files
  • Monitoring agents fingerprinting /etc/passwd
  • A developer debugging DB connectivity by grepping the config
Suppression filter
| where not (InitiatingProcessFileName matches regex @"(?i)/(sh|bash|dash)$" and InitiatingProcessCommandLine has_any ("backup","deploy","monitor"))
Response runbook
1) Triage: confirm the parent chain traces to php-fpm/apache (not an interactive admin shell) and check the acting user; interactive admin activity is likely benign. 2) Contain: if www-data-initiated, isolate the host, rotate the YesWiki DB credentials in wakka.config.php and any secrets in .env, and force-reset affected accounts. 3) Hunt: check for outbound exfiltration (base64/compress → DNS/HTTP egress) from the web user, correlated webshell drops (UC4), and reuse of the leaked DB credentials elsewhere.

YesWiki CalcField exploit attempts — PHP parse/fatal errors from CalcField.php in syslog AIExploitation Low
Hunts PHP 'Parse error', 'syntax error', 'Fatal error', or 'undefined function' messages originating from CalcField.php in forwarded PHP/Apache error logs — the tell of failed regex-bypass fuzzing against the eval() sink before a working RCE payload lands. Captures attempts that succeed at hitting eval() but fail to execute cleanly. Rationale: The article's core flaw is regex-then-eval, so a bypass attempt that reaches eval() with malformed PHP produces parse/fatal errors referencing CalcField.php; clustering these errors surfaces active fuzzing that clean web-log signatures miss. Cross-checked against: • https://github.com/advisories/GHSA-px5m-h76g-p7p8 • https://github.com/YesWiki/yeswiki/security/advisories/GHSA-px5m-h76g-p7p8
ATT&CKT1059.004 T1190
Data sources
Expected false positives · estimated rate: medium — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • A genuine buggy calc formula authored by a legitimate form designer producing a one-off parse error
  • A YesWiki version-mismatch/plugin bug throwing CalcField errors unrelated to attack
  • Log-noise from an unrelated PHP file that happens to reference 'CalcField' in a stack trace
  • PHP upgrade changing function availability (undefined function noise) after a maintenance window
Response runbook
1) Triage: read the surrounding error lines to recover the offending formula string and the source request/IP from correlated web logs (UC1/UC2); repeated errors from one source = active fuzzing. 2) Contain: block the source IP at the WAF and prioritize the 4.6.6 upgrade; virtual-patch the Bazar save endpoint. 3) Hunt: pivot to endpoint UCs (UC3/UC4/UC5) to confirm whether any attempt progressed to code execution, and review for a subsequent error-free save (the likely successful payload).

YesWiki BazarImportAction object-injection exploit request (CVE-2026-52777) AIExploitation High
Hunts inbound POST requests to the YesWiki BazaR importer endpoint (?BazaR&vue=importer) that carry the vulnerable importfiche parameter, the exact request shape an attacker uses to reach the unserialize() sink in CSVManager.php. Article-specific because it keys on YesWiki's own routing string rather than a generic deserialization pattern. Rationale: Uses YesWiki's exact routing tokens BazaR + vue=importer (from BazarAction::run VOIR_IMPORTER -> callAction('bazarimport')) plus POST method, which is the only path that reaches CSVManager::importEntry. Cross-checked GitLab advisory and YesWiki issue #356. Cross-checked against: • https://advisories.gitlab.com/composer/yeswiki/yeswiki/CVE-2026-52777/ • https://github.com/YesWiki/yeswiki/issues/356
ATT&CKT1190
Data sourcesWeb
Expected false positives · estimated rate: low — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Legitimate admin using the Bazar CSV import UI to import entries
  • Vulnerability scanners (Nuclei/Burp) probing the importer endpoint
  • Security team validating the CVE-2026-52777 patch on 4.6.6
  • Automated content-migration scripts that POST to the importer
  • Uptime/synthetic monitors that replay a saved import request
Suppression filter
| where csUserAgent !has "Nuclei" and csUserAgent !has "Burp" and cIP !in ("<known-scanner-ips>")
Response runbook
1) Triage: pull the full request for the matched cIP/csUserName; confirm request body contained importfiche[] and whether the source is an internal admin workstation or an external/unknown IP, and check the Referer for a cross-site origin (CSRF). 2) Contain: if body carried a base64 blob or the source is untrusted, block the source IP at the WAF and force-logout/rotate the admin session; verify the host is on YesWiki >=4.6.6. 3) Hunt: search same host for php-fpm/apache spawning shells and for wakka.config.php or *.php writes under the webroot in the following 30 minutes.

| where csMethod == "POST"
| where csUriQuery has "BazaR" and csUriQuery has "vue=importer"
| project TimeGenerated, Computer, cIP, csMethod, csUriStem, csUriQuery, csUserName, scStatus, csUserAgent
| sort by TimeGenerated desc

Base64 PHP-serialized-object payload in importfiche POST body AIExploitation High
Detects the deserialization payload itself: a request to a YesWiki host whose body contains the importfiche parameter alongside a base64 string that decodes to a PHP serialized object (prefixes Tzo = 'O:' object, YToxOnt = 'a:1:{' array as in the PoC). This is the highest-fidelity signal that an actual object-injection payload (e.g. a PHPGGC Doctrine chain) was sent, not just endpoint probing. Rationale: Combines the article's exact sink-feeding param name (importfiche, from BazarImportAction formatArguments) with base64 markers of PHP serialization grammar (Tzo/YToxOnt) exercised by base64_decode+unserialize; the PoC payload itself begins YToxOnt. Requires a WAF that logs the POST body, noted as a deployment prerequisite. Cross-checked against: • https://advisories.gitlab.com/composer/yeswiki/yeswiki/CVE-2026-52777/ • https://github.com/ambionics/phpggc
ATT&CKT1190 T1059
Data sourcesWeb

  • Security researcher submitting benign serialized test objects
  • Pen-test / red-team validating CVE-2026-52777 with PHPGGC
  • WAF replaying a captured malicious request during tuning
Response runbook
1) Triage: base64-decode the matched importfiche value; if it decodes to O:<n>:"<Class>" confirm the class (e.g. Doctrine\*) and whether it is a known PHPGGC gadget. 2) Contain: block the source at the WAF, isolate the YesWiki host pending review, and rotate the targeted admin session/credentials; patch to >=4.6.6. 3) Hunt: on the host, look for php-fpm/apache child shells, new webshells under the webroot, and outbound connections initiated by the web-server user in the minutes after the request.

YesWiki web-server process spawning an OS shell (deserialization RCE outcome) AIExploitation High
Detects the payoff of a successful PHPGGC Doctrine/RCE1 chain: the YesWiki web-server process (php-fpm/apache2/httpd/nginx) spawning a shell or download/exec utility. On a normal YesWiki host these processes never fork /bin/sh, curl, wget or python. Rationale: The article states Doctrine/RCE1 terminates in system($cmd); the observable is the web-server process forking a shell/downloader, which on a PHP wiki host is essentially never benign. Parent set (php-fpm/apache2/httpd/nginx) is article/stack-specific. Cross-checked against: • https://advisories.gitlab.com/composer/yeswiki/yeswiki/CVE-2026-52777/ • https://github.com/ambionics/phpggc
ATT&CKT1059.004 T1190

  • Deployment or backup scripts run under the web-server user
  • Composer/npm build steps executed by the web account during updates
  • Health-check scripts invoking curl from the app tier

| where ProcessCommandLine !has "ImageMagick" and ProcessCommandLine !has "/usr/bin/convert" and not (FileName in~ ("curl","wget") and ProcessCommandLine has "healthcheck")
Response runbook
1) Triage: inspect the child command line and the php-fpm parent; determine if it maps to a known plugin/cron or is an ad-hoc shell (id/whoami/reverse-shell). 2) Contain: kill the process tree, isolate the host, and preserve the php-fpm worker for forensics; block any C2 IP seen. 3) Hunt: enumerate files written by the web-server user (webshells, wakka.config.php), review MySQL access, and pivot to other sites on the same shared host.
DeviceProcessEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(30d)
| where InitiatingProcessFileName in~ ("php-fpm","php-fpm7.4","php-fpm8.1","php-fpm8.2","httpd","apache2","nginx","php")
| where FileName in~ ("sh","bash","dash","ksh","curl","wget","python","python3","perl","nc","ncat")
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, AccountName, InitiatingProcessFileName, InitiatingProcessCommandLine, FileName, ProcessCommandLine, SHA256
| sort by Timestamp desc
ImProcessCreate
| where TimeGenerated > ago(30d)
| where ParentProcessName has_any ("php-fpm","httpd","apache2","nginx")
| where ActingProcessName has_any ("/sh","/bash","/dash","/curl","/wget","/python","/perl","/nc")
| project TimeGenerated, DvcHostname, ActorUsername, ParentProcessName, ParentProcessCommandLine, ActingProcessName, ActingProcessCommandLine
| sort by TimeGenerated desc

YesWiki wakka.config.php modified by web-server account (post-RCE persistence) AIInstallation High
Alerts when YesWiki's core config file wakka.config.php is created/modified by a web-server process (php-fpm/apache/nginx). The advisory names wakka.config.php as an explicit post-exploitation target; that file is not rewritten by the web tier during normal operation, so a web-server-initiated write is a strong persistence/tamper signal. Rationale: Advisory Impact section explicitly lists modifying wakka.config.php as an attacker post-exploitation action; the file+web-process-initiator pairing is high-fidelity because the web tier does not rewrite core config in normal use. Cross-checked against: • https://advisories.gitlab.com/composer/yeswiki/yeswiki/CVE-2026-52777/
ATT&CKT1505.003
Data sourcesEndpoint.Filesystem
Expected false positives · estimated rate: low — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Admin running the YesWiki installer/updater under the web-server user which rewrites wakka.config.php
  • A legitimate config-change action performed through the wiki admin UI
  • Automated provisioning/IaC re-templating the config file
  • Migration to 4.6.6 that touches the config during upgrade
Suppression filter
| where InitiatingProcessCommandLine !has "install" and InitiatingProcessCommandLine !has "update" and InitiatingProcessCommandLine !has "upgrade"
Response runbook
1) Triage: diff the new wakka.config.php against the last known-good version; check for injected PHP, altered DB creds, or debug/eval flags, and correlate with an importfiche POST in the prior 30 min. 2) Contain: restore the vetted config, isolate the host, and rotate DB and admin credentials; upgrade to >=4.6.6. 3) Hunt: scan the webroot for newly written *.php (webshells), review recent web-server-spawned processes, and inspect MySQL for unauthorized dumps.

| where InitiatingProcessFileName has_any ("php-fpm","httpd","apache2","nginx","php")
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, FolderPath, FileName, ActionType, InitiatingProcessFileName, InitiatingProcessCommandLine, InitiatingProcessAccountName
| sort by Timestamp desc

| where ActingProcessName has_any ("php-fpm","httpd","apache2","nginx","php")
| project TimeGenerated, DvcHostname, ActorUsername, ActingProcessName, ActingProcessCommandLine, TargetFilePath, EventType
| sort by TimeGenerated desc

YesWiki unauthenticated erasespamedcomments page-deletion invocation (CVE-2026-52766) AIExploitation High
Hunts POST requests to a YesWiki instance that reference the `erasespamedcomments` action together with the `clean`/`suppr[]` deletion parameters, the exact request shape from the CVE-2026-52766 PoC. Because the action performs no authorization or CSRF check, any single such request from an unauthenticated source is a live exploitation attempt for arbitrary wiki page deletion (including PagePrincipale). Rationale: Uses the CVE-specific action name `erasespamedcomments` plus the `suppr[]`/`clean=yes` deletion parameters from the advisory PoC (POST /?wiki=SpamCleanup, clean=yes&suppr[0]=...). The action name is unique to YesWiki and the parameter trio is otherwise never seen, giving a near-zero-FP signature; requires a log source that captures POST body/full query (WAF or app log) since IIS alone omits the body. Cross-checked against: • https://github.com/advisories/GHSA-6x7x-gcmf-7r8x • https://nvd.nist.gov/vuln/detail/CVE-2026-52766
ATT&CKT1190 T1485
Data sourcesWeb.Web
Expected false positives · estimated rate: low — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Authenticated wiki admin legitimately running spam-comment cleanup after a spam wave
  • Security scanner / DAST tool (Burp, Nuclei) firing a CVE-2026-52766 test request in an authorized pentest
  • Vulnerability-management team validating the patch on a staging YesWiki host
  • A WAF replay/allow-list health check that reissues a captured deletion request
Suppression filter
| where csUserName == "" or isempty(csUserName)   // keep only unauthenticated callers; authenticated admin cleanup is expected
Response runbook
1) Triage: pull the full request for the matching cIP/src — confirm it is unauthenticated (empty csUserName) and enumerate the tags inside suppr[]; check whether PagePrincipale or admin pages are named. 2) Contain: if unauthenticated and unexpected, block the source IP at the WAF, put the YesWiki instance into hibernation (WIKI_IN_HIBERNATION) or take it offline, and confirm the app is upgraded to >=4.6.6. 3) Hunt: search all access logs from the same src for the preceding trigger-page creation (POST to */edit carrying {{erasespamedcomments}}) and for a 404 spike on the deleted tags; restore affected pages from DB/page-history backup.
W3CIISLog
| where TimeGenerated > ago(7d)
| where csMethod == "POST"
| where csUriStem has "erasespamedcomments" or csUriQuery has_any ("erasespamedcomments","suppr","clean=yes")
| project TimeGenerated, cIP, csMethod, sSiteName, csUriStem, csUriQuery, scStatus, csUserName, csUserAgent, Computer
| order by TimeGenerated desc
