YesWiki confirmed mass page deletion — bulk 'Suppression de la page' / deletion-request burst (CVE-2026-52766) AIActions on Objectives Medium
Hunts the impact stage of CVE-2026-52766: a burst of confirmed page deletions in a short window, either as YesWiki admin-log 'Suppression de la page' entries (application log) or as a spike of erasespamedcomments/suppr deletion POSTs from one source. Legitimate admin cleanup touches 1-3 pages; mass abuse deletes many tags in one automated run. Rationale: Pivots on the exact admin-log string `Suppression de la page` written by PageController::delete()->LogAdministrativeAction (article code), and on a per-source burst of suppr/erasespamedcomments POSTs. Volume + the CVE-specific action string separates automated mass deletion from routine single-page maintenance; the app-log path also confirms deletions actually succeeded rather than merely being attempted. Cross-checked against: • https://github.com/advisories/GHSA-6x7x-gcmf-7r8x • https://nvd.nist.gov/vuln/detail/CVE-2026-52766
ATT&CKT1485
Data sourcesWeb.Web
Expected false positives · estimated rate: low — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Wiki admin performing a large legitimate content purge/migration (decommissioning a namespace)
  • Scripted maintenance job that deletes stale pages in bulk on a schedule
  • Restore/reimport operation that deletes-then-recreates many pages
  • Spam wave genuinely being cleaned by an authorized moderator using the intended feature
Response runbook
1) Triage: expand the make_set of SamplePages / suppr tags to see which pages were deleted and whether PagePrincipale, admin, or other users' pages are included; correlate to the source IP and whether it was authenticated. 2) Contain: hibernate or isolate the YesWiki host, block the source IP, and confirm the upgrade to >=4.6.6 (or apply an ACL gating erasespamedcomments to admins). 3) Hunt: pull page-history/DB backups and restore deleted tags; check for the initial trigger-page creation and for follow-on defacement or re-creation of the front page by the same source.
Syslog
| where TimeGenerated > ago(1d)
| where SyslogMessage has "Suppression de la page"
| summarize DeletedPages = count(), SamplePages = make_set(SyslogMessage, 50), FirstSeen = min(TimeGenerated), LastSeen = max(TimeGenerated) by HostName, ProcessName, bin(TimeGenerated, 10m)
| where DeletedPages > 5   // >5 confirmed page deletions in a 10-min window — far above manual admin cleanup (typ. 1-3)
| order by DeletedPages desc
WEB
Toggle if your env has no CIM data-model acceleration.
| tstats `summariesonly` count from datamodel=Web where Web.http_method=POST AND (Web.url="*erasespamedcomments*" OR Web.uri_query="*erasespamedcomments*" OR Web.uri_query="*suppr*" OR Web.url="*suppr*") by Web.src, Web.dest, _time span=10m
| `drop_dm_object_name(Web)`
| where count > 5
| sort - count
| tstats summariesonly=false count from datamodel=Web where Web.http_method=POST AND (Web.url="*erasespamedcomments*" OR Web.uri_query="*erasespamedcomments*" OR Web.uri_query="*suppr*" OR Web.url="*suppr*") by Web.src, Web.dest, _time span=10m
| `drop_dm_object_name(Web)`
| where count > 5
| sort - count
YesWiki page-deletion aftermath — 404 spike on previously-valid wiki pages (CVE-2026-52766) AIActions on Objectives Medium
Detects the downstream impact of CVE-2026-52766: pages deleted by the erasespamedcomments abuse now return HTTP 404 to normal visitors. A sudden spike of 404s across many distinct wiki page paths in a short window — especially minutes after an erasespamedcomments POST — indicates successful mass deletion. Rationale: Uses the YesWiki URL shape (`?wiki=<PageTag>`) plus a 404 status spike across many distinct page tags, which is the observable end state after PageManager::deleteOrphaned() wipes pages/links/acls/tags rows. Best deployed as a same-source time-window correlation with UC1's erasespamedcomments POST to cut ambiguity from ordinary broken-link 404s. Cross-checked against: • https://github.com/advisories/GHSA-6x7x-gcmf-7r8x • https://nvd.nist.gov/vuln/detail/CVE-2026-52766
ATT&CKT1485
Data sourcesWeb.Web
Expected false positives · estimated rate: medium — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Broken-link crawler / SEO bot hitting many stale URLs
  • Legitimate content restructure where pages were intentionally renamed or removed
  • A vulnerability scanner enumerating non-existent wiki page tags
  • Cache/CDN warm-up requesting pages that legitimately never existed
Suppression filter
| where csUriStem has_any ("wiki") | where DistinctPages > 10 and NotFound > 20   // require both breadth (distinct pages) and volume to suppress lone broken-link crawlers
Response runbook
1) Triage: list the distinct 404 page tags and check whether any were serving 200 in the hours before the spike (a genuine deletion signature) versus never-existed paths (scanner noise). 2) Contain: if prior-200 pages are now 404, treat as confirmed destruction — isolate the host, block the abusing source from UC1/UC2, and confirm patch >=4.6.6. 3) Hunt: correlate the 404 tags to the suppr[] array values in the preceding erasespamedcomments POST from the same window/source, then restore the affected pages from backup and monitor for re-deletion.
W3CIISLog
| where TimeGenerated > ago(1d)
| where csMethod == "GET"
| where scStatus == 404
| where csUriStem has "wiki" or csUriQuery has "wiki"
| summarize NotFound = count(), DistinctPages = dcount(csUriQuery), Pages = make_set(csUriQuery, 50) by Computer, sSiteName, bin(TimeGenerated, 15m)
| where DistinctPages > 10   // >10 distinct previously-served wiki pages now 404 in a 15-min window — deletion aftermath
| order by NotFound desc
WEB
Toggle if your env has no CIM data-model acceleration.
| tstats `summariesonly` count from datamodel=Web where Web.http_method=GET AND Web.status=404 AND (Web.url="*wiki=*" OR Web.uri_query="*wiki=*") by Web.dest, Web.uri_query, _time span=15m
| `drop_dm_object_name(Web)`
| stats sum(count) as notFound dc(uri_query) as distinctPages values(uri_query) as pages by dest, _time
| where distinctPages > 10
| sort - notFound
| tstats summariesonly=false count from datamodel=Web where Web.http_method=GET AND Web.status=404 AND (Web.url="*wiki=*" OR Web.uri_query="*wiki=*") by Web.dest, Web.uri_query, _time span=15m
| `drop_dm_object_name(Web)`
| stats sum(count) as notFound dc(uri_query) as distinctPages values(uri_query) as pages by dest, _time
| where distinctPages > 10
| sort - notFound

Compromised @injectivelabs/sdk-ts exfiltrates wallet keys through fake telemetry

Aikido
2026-07-09 8 use cases 3 techniques 6 kill-chain phases detected

A malicious release of @injectivelabs/sdk-ts hid a wallet-key stealer inside code labeled as usage telemetry, then spread it across 17 more npm packages. Here's how it worked and how to check your projects. Category: Vulnerabilities & Threats

Detected
Reconnaissance. Attacker researches the target — OSINT, scanning, enumeration.
Weaponization. Coupling exploit code with deliverable payload (e.g. weaponized PDF/Office doc, trojanized installer).
Delivery. Transmitting the weapon (phishing email, USB, watering hole, drive-by, malicious ad). → [LLM] Transitive install of poisoned @injectivelabs 1.20.21 build under node_modules
Exploitation. Triggering the exploit — vulnerability/macro/trust abuse to execute code. → Article-specific behavioural hunt — Compromised @injectivelabs/sdk-ts exfiltrates wallet keys through fake telemetry
Installation. Establishing persistence on the host — backdoor, service, scheduled task, registry key. → [LLM] Malicious @injectivelabs SDK build artifact by SHA-256 on disk · Suspicious browser extension installation · File hash IOCs — endpoint file/process match
Command & Control. Beacon to attacker infrastructure for control and tasking. → [LLM] Exfil to lookalike Injective gRPC-web subdomain (@injectivelabs stealer C2) · Network connections to article IPs / domains
Actions on Objectives. Lateral movement, credential dumping, data theft, ransomware, sabotage. → Infostealer — non-browser process accessing browser cookie/login DBs
Exfil to lookalike Injective gRPC-web subdomain (@injectivelabs stealer C2) AICommand & Control High
Hunts outbound DNS/network activity to testnet.archival.chain.grpc-web.injective.network, the character-code-rebuilt exfil host used by the trojanized @injectivelabs/sdk-ts@1.20.21 to smuggle base64 wallet key material inside an X-Request-Id header disguised as gRPC-web traffic. Article-specific because the FQDN is a fixed IOC unique to this campaign. Rationale: The exfil FQDN testnet.archival.chain.grpc-web.injective.network is a fixed, campaign-unique IOC (a lookalike subdomain never served by real Injective infra); matching it exactly avoids the FP risk of the parent injective.network.
ATT&CKT1071.001 T1132.001 T1041 T1001.003
Data sourcesNetwork_Resolution.DNS Network_Traffic.All_Traffic
Expected false positives · estimated rate: low — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • A legitimate future Injective testnet archival endpoint being stood up under this exact FQDN (verify DNS/PKI ownership)
  • Security tooling / sandbox detonating the malicious package intentionally
  • Threat-intel sinkhole or research VM deliberately resolving the IOC
  • Internal DNS logging replaying old cached queries
Response runbook
1) Triage: confirm the resolving host ran an @injectivelabs-dependent app; capture the initiating process (node.exe) and user. 2) Contain: block the FQDN at DNS/proxy/firewall, isolate the host, and treat every wallet mnemonic/private key derived on it as exposed — freeze/rotate. 3) Hunt: pivot to all hosts querying the FQDN, pull package-lock/yarn.lock for @injectivelabs/*@1.20.21, and search DeviceFileEvents for the two malicious build artifacts.
DeviceNetworkEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(30d)
| where RemoteUrl has "testnet.archival.chain.grpc-web.injective.network"
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, InitiatingProcessFileName, InitiatingProcessCommandLine, InitiatingProcessAccountName, RemoteUrl, RemoteIP, RemotePort
| order by Timestamp desc
ImDnsActivity
| where TimeGenerated > ago(30d)
| where DnsQuery has "testnet.archival.chain.grpc-web.injective.network"
| project TimeGenerated, DvcHostname, SrcIpAddr, SrcHostname, DnsQuery, DnsResponseName, DnsResponseCodeName
| order by TimeGenerated desc

Malicious @injectivelabs SDK build artifact by SHA-256 on disk AIInstallation Medium
Detects the two poisoned build files (accounts-Cy0p4lLW.cjs / accounts-jQ1GSgaW.js) from @injectivelabs/sdk-ts@1.20.21 landing on disk, matched on their exact SHA-256 hashes. High fidelity IOC match that survives file renaming. Rationale: Both SHA-256 values are published IOCs for the exact malicious build artifacts; a hash match is unambiguous and near-zero FP, catching the stealer even if the file is renamed during transitive install.
ATT&CKT1195.002 T1027
Data sourcesEndpoint.Filesystem
Expected false positives · estimated rate: low — model-assessed, tune to your environment

Transitive install of poisoned @injectivelabs 1.20.21 build under node_modules AIDelivery Medium
Structural supply-chain detection: the campaign-unique build filenames accounts-Cy0p4lLW.cjs / accounts-jQ1GSgaW.js appearing under a node_modules/@injectivelabs path. Resilient to re-signing/re-hash because it keys on the version-marker filenames + package scope rather than the SHA-256, catching victims who pulled the stealer transitively via any of the 18 sibling packages. Rationale: The build filenames accounts-Cy0p4lLW.cjs / accounts-jQ1GSgaW.js are unique to the poisoned 1.20.21 dist and act as a version marker; combined with the node_modules/@injectivelabs scope this flags transitive victims (e.g. via wallet-core) who never named sdk-ts directly, and survives re-hash of the still-downloadable deprecated package.
ATT&CKT1195.002
Data sourcesEndpoint.Filesystem
Expected false positives · estimated rate: low — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Aikido/other scanner replaying the artifact during a rescan
  • Developer intentionally checking out the compromised version to reproduce/analyze
  • A future clean @injectivelabs build coincidentally reusing the same hashed chunk name (unlikely — Rollup chunk hashes are content-derived)
Response runbook
1) Triage: on each hit, read the package's package.json version and lockfile to confirm 1.20.21 was resolved (directly or transitively). 2) Contain: delete node_modules, repin @injectivelabs/* to >=1.20.23, and rebuild; flag any wallet keys/seed phrases derived on the host for rotation. 3) Hunt: enumerate every repo/CI job with @injectivelabs/*@1.20.21 in lockfiles and correlate hosts against exfil-domain contacts and the SHA-256 file detection.
DeviceFileEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(30d)
| where FileName in~ ("accounts-Cy0p4lLW.cjs", "accounts-jQ1GSgaW.js")
| where FolderPath contains "node_modules" and FolderPath contains "injectivelabs"
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, ActionType, FileName, FolderPath, SHA256, InitiatingProcessFileName, InitiatingProcessCommandLine, InitiatingProcessAccountName
| order by Timestamp desc
ImFileEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(30d)
| where TargetFileName in~ ("accounts-Cy0p4lLW.cjs", "accounts-jQ1GSgaW.js")
| where TargetFilePath contains "node_modules" and TargetFilePath contains "injectivelabs"
| project TimeGenerated, DvcHostname, ActorUsername, ActingProcessName, ActingProcessCommandLine, TargetFilePath, TargetFileName, TargetFileSHA256
| order by TimeGenerated desc

id: 7c8b2e10-4d4f-4a8c-9c1f-bf6e2c4a8d01

File hash IOCs — endpoint file/process match Installation High
Match SHA256/SHA1/MD5 named in the article against EDR file/process telemetry.
ATT&CKT1027
Data sourcesEndpoint.Filesystem Endpoint.Processes DeviceFileEvents DeviceProcessEvents
// Pre-filter each table BEFORE the union — the engine cannot push
// predicates across `union`, and DeviceFileEvents lacks ProcessCommandLine
// (Initiating only) so column-projection has to differ per side.
union
    ( DeviceFileEvents
        | where Timestamp > ago(7d)
        | where InitiatingProcessAccountName !endswith "$"
        | where SHA256 in~ ("103c4e6181151c1bcfedc41506cd1815458c38375d08a8fcd9981dbe0b965ce0", "9a59eb454f3ca3fe91214136ee5edd417cc47a80e6f169b52099d6561944baf9") or SHA1 in~ ("103c4e6181151c1bcfedc41506cd1815458c38375d08a8fcd9981dbe0b965ce0", "9a59eb454f3ca3fe91214136ee5edd417cc47a80e6f169b52099d6561944baf9") or MD5 in~ ("103c4e6181151c1bcfedc41506cd1815458c38375d08a8fcd9981dbe0b965ce0", "9a59eb454f3ca3fe91214136ee5edd417cc47a80e6f169b52099d6561944baf9")
        | project Timestamp, DeviceName, ActionType, FileName, FolderPath, SHA256,
                  Cmd = InitiatingProcessCommandLine, Source = "DeviceFileEvents" ),
    ( DeviceProcessEvents
        | where Timestamp > ago(7d)
        | where AccountName !endswith "$"
        | where SHA256 in~ ("103c4e6181151c1bcfedc41506cd1815458c38375d08a8fcd9981dbe0b965ce0", "9a59eb454f3ca3fe91214136ee5edd417cc47a80e6f169b52099d6561944baf9") or SHA1 in~ ("103c4e6181151c1bcfedc41506cd1815458c38375d08a8fcd9981dbe0b965ce0", "9a59eb454f3ca3fe91214136ee5edd417cc47a80e6f169b52099d6561944baf9") or MD5 in~ ("103c4e6181151c1bcfedc41506cd1815458c38375d08a8fcd9981dbe0b965ce0", "9a59eb454f3ca3fe91214136ee5edd417cc47a80e6f169b52099d6561944baf9")
        | project Timestamp, DeviceName, ActionType, FileName, FolderPath, SHA256,
                  Cmd = ProcessCommandLine, Source = "DeviceProcessEvents" )
| order by Timestamp desc

// Pre-filter both ASIM tables before the union — same pattern as the
// Defender version so the engine can push hash predicates per-side.
let BadHashes = dynamic(["103c4e6181151c1bcfedc41506cd1815458c38375d08a8fcd9981dbe0b965ce0", "9a59eb454f3ca3fe91214136ee5edd417cc47a80e6f169b52099d6561944baf9"]);
union
    ( ImFileEvent
        | where TimeGenerated > ago(7d)
        | where ActorUsername !endswith "$"
        | where TargetFileSHA256 in~ (BadHashes)
           or TargetFileSHA1 in~ (BadHashes)
           or TargetFileMD5 in~ (BadHashes)
        | project TimeGenerated, DvcHostname, EventType,
                  TargetFileName, TargetFilePath, TargetFileSHA256,
                  Cmd = ActingProcessName, Source = "ImFileEvent" ),
    ( ImProcessCreate
        | where TimeGenerated > ago(7d)
        | where ActorUsername !endswith "$"
        | where SHA256 in~ (BadHashes) or SHA1 in~ (BadHashes) or MD5 in~ (BadHashes)
        | project TimeGenerated, DvcHostname, EventType = TargetProcessName,
                  TargetFileName = TargetProcessName, TargetFilePath = TargetProcessName,
                  TargetFileSHA256 = SHA256,
                  Cmd = TargetProcessCommandLine, Source = "ImProcessCreate" )
| order by TimeGenerated desc

Reconnaissance. Attacker researches the target — OSINT, scanning, enumeration.
Weaponization. Coupling exploit code with deliverable payload (e.g. weaponized PDF/Office doc, trojanized installer).
Delivery. Transmitting the weapon (phishing email, USB, watering hole, drive-by, malicious ad).
Exploitation. Triggering the exploit — vulnerability/macro/trust abuse to execute code. → Article-specific behavioural hunt — One Target, Two Flags | Rival Espionage Actors Converge On Pakistani Law Enforce
Installation. Establishing persistence on the host — backdoor, service, scheduled task, registry key.
Command & Control. Beacon to attacker infrastructure for control and tasking. → [LLM] Outbound C2 to PlugX/ShadowPad/Cobalt Strike/Remcos infrastructure targeting Pakistani law enforcement · [LLM] Compromised web-application server beaconing to espionage C2 (portal-update implant) · Beaconing — periodic outbound to small set of destinations · Network connections to article IPs / domains
Actions on Objectives. Lateral movement, credential dumping, data theft, ransomware, sabotage.
Outbound C2 to PlugX/ShadowPad/Cobalt Strike/Remcos infrastructure targeting Pakistani law enforcement AICommand & Control High
Hunts any internal host establishing outbound connections to the 13 C2 IPs SentinelLABS attributed to the four tooling clusters (PlugX, ShadowPad, Cobalt Strike, Remcos) converging on Balochistan Police and other Pakistani law-enforcement orgs between Feb 2024 and Apr 2026. Pure network-IOC match on disclosed espionage C2 servers. Rationale: Anchored on the exact 13 C2 IPs from Table 1 / code blocks (PlugX 172.111.233.x + 172.94.9.x + 45.74.6.17, ShadowPad 45.125.32.218, Cobalt Strike 142.171.183.8 + 193.42.25.65, Remcos 89.31.121.220). Any egress to these known-bad hosts is high-fidelity; the tooling families and Pakistani-entity victimology are corroborated externally, though the specific IPs are from the SentinelLABS primary report only. Cross-checked against: • https://www.sentinelone.com/labs/one-target-china-india-espionage-converge-on-pakistani-law-enforcement/ • https://malpedia.caad.fkie.fraunhofer.de/details/win.shadowpad • https://thehackernews.com/2023/07/pakistani-entities-targeted-in.html
ATT&CKT1071.001 T1573 T1219
Data sourcesNetwork_Traffic.All_Traffic
Expected false positives · estimated rate: low — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Security researcher / threat-intel analyst deliberately sandboxing or sinkholing one of these IPs from a corporate host
  • IP reassignment after takedown — a benign service later hosted on a recycled VPS IP (172.94.9.x / 45.x hosting ranges are commodity VPS)
  • Internal threat-intel validation tooling or EDR connectivity checks pinging the IOC list
  • Proxy/NAT concentration causing many internal hosts to appear as one src toward the IP
Suppression filter
| where InitiatingProcessFileName !in~ ("MsSense.exe","MsMpEng.exe","SenseIR.exe") // exclude EDR/AV connectivity-check processes
Response runbook
1) Triage: confirm the connection is genuinely outbound and established (not a blocked/attempt), identify the initiating process and host role — servers hosting the CMS/FIR/HRMIS/HotelEye/CRMS apps are highest priority. 2) Contain: block all 13 IPs at perimeter, isolate the host, snapshot memory before reboot to preserve PlugX/ShadowPad in-memory implants. 3) Hunt: pivot on the host for DLL side-loading (unsigned DLL next to a signed EXE), scheduled tasks/Run keys created near first-seen, and lateral SMB/RDP from the host; sweep the org for any other host touching the same /24s (172.111.233.0/24, 172.94.9.0/24).
let C2 = dynamic(["172.111.233.36","172.111.233.96","172.111.233.12","172.111.233.105","172.111.233.26","172.94.9.49","172.94.9.43","172.94.9.19","45.74.6.17","45.125.32.218","142.171.183.8","193.42.25.65","89.31.121.220"]);
DeviceNetworkEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(30d)
| where RemoteIP in (C2)
| summarize FirstSeen=min(Timestamp), LastSeen=max(Timestamp), ConnCount=count(), Ports=make_set(RemotePort, 20) by DeviceName, RemoteIP, InitiatingProcessFileName, InitiatingProcessFolderPath, InitiatingProcessCommandLine
| order by LastSeen desc
let C2 = dynamic(["172.111.233.36","172.111.233.96","172.111.233.12","172.111.233.105","172.111.233.26","172.94.9.49","172.94.9.43","172.94.9.19","45.74.6.17","45.125.32.218","142.171.183.8","193.42.25.65","89.31.121.220"]);
ImNetworkSession
| where TimeGenerated > ago(30d)
| where DstIpAddr in (C2)
| summarize FirstSeen=min(TimeGenerated), LastSeen=max(TimeGenerated), ConnCount=count(), Ports=make_set(DstPortNumber, 20) by DvcHostname, SrcIpAddr, DstIpAddr, NetworkApplicationProtocol, DvcAction
| order by LastSeen desc

Compromised web-application server beaconing to espionage C2 (portal-update implant) AICommand & Control Medium
Tighter server-side pivot: a web/application-server process (IIS w3wp, Apache/Tomcat java, nginx, php-cgi) on a Pakistani law-enforcement web server initiating outbound to the disclosed C2 IPs. Grounds on the article's China-nexus 'custom implants masquerading as a portal update' planted in one of the citizen/police web applications (e.g. the Complaint Management System). Rationale: Combines the exact C2 IP set with a server-process filter to isolate the article's specific scenario — a China-nexus implant planted in a citizen/police web application (CMS) beaconing out. Web-server processes reaching commodity-VPS C2 IPs is extremely rare and high-fidelity, and directly targets the compromised-webapp vector the article calls out. Cross-checked against: • https://www.sentinelone.com/labs/one-target-china-india-espionage-converge-on-pakistani-law-enforcement/ • https://malpedia.caad.fkie.fraunhofer.de/details/win.shadowpad
ATT&CKT1071.001 T1505.003 T1573
Data sourcesNetwork_Traffic.All_Traffic
Expected false positives · estimated rate: low — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Web app legitimately calling an outbound API that happens to be on a recycled VPS IP after IOC takedown
  • Java-based agent/monitoring on the web server making outbound telemetry calls
  • Server-side update/package fetch (Tomcat/Maven, php composer) to a mirror on the same hosting range
  • App-server health-check or CDN origin-pull to a reassigned address
Suppression filter
| where InitiatingProcessCommandLine !has "maven" and InitiatingProcessCommandLine !has "composer" // exclude server package-manager fetches
Response runbook
1) Triage: identify which web application the process serves (CMS/FIR/HRMIS/AVLS/HotelEye/CRMS) and whether the beacon started after a recent 'portal update'/deployment window; review web-root for recently modified/added handler, JSP, ASPX or PHP files. 2) Contain: take the web app offline or block egress, preserve IIS/Tomcat logs and web-root for forensics, rotate app/service and DB credentials the server can reach. 3) Hunt: search web access logs (W3CIISLog/AppServiceHTTPLogs) for the implant's request pattern, look for webshell-style POSTs, and pivot to any DB export or biometric/criminal-record access from the compromised app identity.

Beaconing — periodic outbound to small set of destinations Command & Control Medium
C2 channel detection via inter-beacon-time stddev / fan-out to single dest.
ATT&CKT1071.001 T1071.004
Data sourcesNetwork_Traffic.All_Traffic DeviceNetworkEvents
DeviceNetworkEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(1d)
| where RemoteIPType == "Public" and ActionType == "ConnectionSuccess"
| project DeviceName, RemoteIP, RemotePort, Timestamp
| sort by DeviceName asc, RemoteIP asc, RemotePort asc, Timestamp asc
| extend prev_dev = prev(DeviceName, 1), prev_ip = prev(RemoteIP, 1),
         prev_port = prev(RemotePort, 1), prev_ts = prev(Timestamp, 1)
| where DeviceName == prev_dev and RemoteIP == prev_ip and RemotePort == prev_port
| extend delta_sec = datetime_diff('second', Timestamp, prev_ts)
| summarize conn_count = count(), avg_delta = avg(delta_sec), stdev_delta = stdev(delta_sec)
    by DeviceName, RemoteIP, RemotePort
| where conn_count > 30 and avg_delta between (30.0 .. 600.0) and stdev_delta < 5.0
| order by conn_count desc
ImNetworkSession
| where TimeGenerated > ago(2h)
| where DvcAction != "Block"
| where ipv4_is_private(DstIpAddr) == false
| summarize ConnCount = count(),
            DistinctMinutes = dcount(bin(TimeGenerated, 1m))
            by DvcHostname, DstIpAddr, DstPortNumber
| where ConnCount > 50 and DistinctMinutes > 30   // sustained, not bursty
| order by ConnCount desc

Symlinks Are Still Scary (And Yes, You Can Commit Them to Git)

Snyk
2026-07-09 5 use cases 2 techniques 4 kill-chain phases detected

A harmless-looking symlink in a Git repo can redirect a tool into reading or writing anywhere on your machine. That old trick is now showing up in AI coding assistants, with nasty results.

Reconnaissance. Attacker researches the target — OSINT, scanning, enumeration. → Asset exposure — vulnerability matches article CVE(s)
Weaponization. Coupling exploit code with deliverable payload (e.g. weaponized PDF/Office doc, trojanized installer).
Delivery. Transmitting the weapon (phishing email, USB, watering hole, drive-by, malicious ad).
Exploitation. Triggering the exploit — vulnerability/macro/trust abuse to execute code. → [LLM] Git-spawned hook execution during recursive clone (CVE-2024-32002) · Trusted vendor binary / installer launching unusual children
Installation. Establishing persistence on the host — backdoor, service, scheduled task, registry key. → [LLM] SSH authorized_keys written by non-SSH tooling (symlink repo payload) · Article-specific behavioural hunt — Symlinks Are Still Scary (And Yes, You Can Commit Them to Git)
Command & Control. Beacon to attacker infrastructure for control and tasking.
Actions on Objectives. Lateral movement, credential dumping, data theft, ransomware, sabotage.
SSH authorized_keys written by non-SSH tooling (symlink repo payload) AIInstallation Medium
Hunts writes/modifications to any user's ~/.ssh/authorized_keys where the writing process is NOT legitimate SSH provisioning tooling — the payoff of the article's headline attack, where a symlink named like project_settings.json checked out from a cloned repo resolves to authorized_keys and a build script/editor/AI coding agent silently writes an attacker key through it. Because the OS resolves the symlink transparently, the file event reports the real target path (.ssh/authorized_keys), which is the tell. Rationale: Anchored on the article's exact payload path ~/.ssh/authorized_keys (code Block 1) written by non-SSH tooling — the symlink resolves so the OS reports the real target, making the write-through observable. Cross-checked MITRE T1098.004, Splunk Security Content and Elastic authorized_keys rules to confirm the technique and avoid duplicating a generic FIM rule by scoping on the writing process. Cross-checked against: • https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1098/004/ • https://research.splunk.com/endpoint/f5ab595e-28e5-4327-8077-5008ba97c850/ • https://www.elastic.co/docs/reference/security/prebuilt-rules/rules/cross-platform/persistence_ssh_authorized_keys_modification
ATT&CKT1098.004 T1195.001
Data sourcesEndpoint.Filesystem
Expected false positives · estimated rate: medium — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Ansible/Puppet/Salt/Terraform pushing authorized_keys via a config-management run (excluded, but custom wrappers may slip through)
  • Developer legitimately running ssh-copy-id or manually editing authorized_keys with vim/nano
  • Cloud-init / provisioning agent seeding keys on first boot of a new VM
  • CI runner injecting a deploy key into ~/.ssh/authorized_keys as an intended step
  • Dotfile-management tools (chezmoi, GNU stow) that symlink or template SSH config
Suppression filter
| where InitiatingProcessFileName !in~ ("terraform","authorized_keys_command","chezmoi","stow") and InitiatingProcessCommandLine !has "ansible"
Response runbook
1) Triage: pull the InitiatingProcess chain — is the writer a dev tool (git, node, python, code, cursor) or shell spawned from a freshly cloned repo path? Compare the written key fingerprint against the user's known keys and check if the file is/was a symlink (ls -l ~/.ssh/authorized_keys, readlink). 2) Contain: if the key is unrecognized, remove the offending authorized_keys line, kill active sessions authenticated by it, and rotate the account; quarantine the source repo. 3) Hunt: search the same host/user for the source symlink (git ls-files -s | grep '^120000'), other writes to ~/.ssh, ~/.bashrc, ~/.git/hooks, and any inbound SSH logons using the added key.
DeviceFileEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(14d)
| where FolderPath endswith "/.ssh/authorized_keys" or (FileName == "authorized_keys" and FolderPath has "/.ssh")
| where ActionType in ("FileCreated","FileModified","FileRenamed")
| where InitiatingProcessAccountName !endswith "$"
| where InitiatingProcessFileName !in~ ("sshd","ssh","ssh-keygen","ssh-copy-id","cloud-init","useradd","adduser","ansible","puppet","chef-client","salt-minion")
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, InitiatingProcessAccountName, FileName, FolderPath, InitiatingProcessFileName, InitiatingProcessFolderPath, InitiatingProcessCommandLine, InitiatingProcessParentFileName, SHA256
| order by Timestamp desc
ImFileEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(14d)
| where TargetFilePath endswith "/.ssh/authorized_keys" or (TargetFileName == "authorized_keys" and TargetFilePath has "/.ssh")
| where EventType in ("FileCreated","FileModified","FileRename")
| where not(ActingProcessName has_any ("sshd","ssh-keygen","ssh-copy-id","cloud-init","ansible","puppet","salt-minion"))
| project TimeGenerated, DvcHostname, ActorUsername, TargetFilePath, TargetFileName, ActingProcessName, ActingProcessCommandLine
| order by TimeGenerated desc

Git-spawned hook execution during recursive clone (CVE-2024-32002) AIExploitation High
Hunts a process whose image lives inside a .git/hooks/ directory and whose parent is git — the exact signature of CVE-2024-32002, where a malicious repository's crafted submodule + symlink writes a hook into .git/ that git executes while the clone is still running, yielding RCE from nothing more than git clone --recurse-submodules. No build step or 'run the project' required. Rationale: Anchored on the CVE-2024-32002 mechanic named in the article (git clone --recurse-submodules dropping a script into .git/hooks and running it during clone). The parent=git + child-image-in-.git/hooks pair is high-fidelity because hooks are not supposed to execute during a clone; confirmed via the git security advisory GHSA-8h77-4q3w-gfgv and Amal Murali's PoC writeup. Cross-checked against: • https://github.com/git/git/security/advisories/GHSA-8h77-4q3w-gfgv • https://amalmurali.me/posts/git-rce/ • https://www.helpnetsecurity.com/2024/05/16/git-cve-2024-32002/
ATT&CKT1195.001 T1059.004
Data sourcesEndpoint.Processes
Expected false positives · estimated rate: low — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Developer with legitimately installed local git hooks (post-checkout/post-merge) firing during a normal pull or checkout
  • Husky / pre-commit framework hooks that shell out during commit or checkout operations
  • CI systems that intentionally invoke repo hooks as part of a pipeline stage
  • git-lfs post-checkout smudge hooks running on a large-file repo clone
  • Monorepo tooling (e.g. Nx, Turborepo) that registers checkout hooks
Suppression filter
| where not (FolderPath has_any ("husky","git-lfs","post-merge") or InitiatingProcessCommandLine has_any ("pull","checkout HEAD","lfs"))
Response runbook
1) Triage: inspect the executed hook file under .git/hooks/ and the InitiatingProcessCommandLine — confirm it was a clone/--recurse-submodules op and read the hook body for network callbacks or key writes. Check git version on host against the patched set (>=2.39.4/2.40.2/2.41.1/2.42.2/2.43.4/2.44.1/2.45.1). 2) Contain: isolate the host, kill the hook process tree, and quarantine the cloned repo directory; block the source repo URL. 3) Hunt: on the same host look for downstream child processes of the hook, writes to ~/.ssh/authorized_keys, new persistence (cron, systemd units, shell rc files), and outbound C2 from the hook's PID.
DeviceProcessEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(14d)
| where FolderPath has_any ("/.git/hooks/", "\\.git\\hooks\\")
| where InitiatingProcessFileName in~ ("git","git.exe","git-remote-https","git-remote-https.exe","bash","sh","dash")
| where InitiatingProcessCommandLine has_any ("clone","submodule","--recurse-submodules") or FolderPath has_any ("post-checkout","post-clone","post-update")
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, AccountName, FileName, FolderPath, ProcessCommandLine, InitiatingProcessFileName, InitiatingProcessCommandLine, InitiatingProcessFolderPath, SHA256
| order by Timestamp desc
ImProcessCreate
| where TimeGenerated > ago(14d)
| where ActingProcessName has_any ("/.git/hooks/", "\\.git\\hooks\\")
| where ParentProcessName has_any ("git","bash","sh","dash")
| where ParentProcessCommandLine has_any ("clone","submodule","--recurse-submodules") or ActingProcessName has_any ("post-checkout","post-clone","post-update")
| project TimeGenerated, DvcHostname, ActorUsername, ActingProcessName, ActingProcessCommandLine, ParentProcessName, ParentProcessCommandLine
| order by TimeGenerated desc

Delivery. Transmitting the weapon (phishing email, USB, watering hole, drive-by, malicious ad). → [LLM] PromptSpy dropper APK sample hash landing on monitored endpoint · Phishing-link click correlated to endpoint execution · Email attachment opened from external sender
Exploitation. Triggering the exploit — vulnerability/macro/trust abuse to execute code. → Office app spawning script/LOLBin child process · Fake CAPTCHA / clipboard-injected PowerShell (ClickFix / FakeCaptcha)
Installation. Establishing persistence on the host — backdoor, service, scheduled task, registry key. → Suspicious browser extension installation · File hash IOCs — endpoint file/process match
Command & Control. Beacon to attacker infrastructure for control and tasking. → [LLM] PromptSpy Android GenAI malware C2/distribution domain contact (mgardownload.com, m-mgarg.com) · Network connections to article IPs / domains

PromptSpy Android GenAI malware C2/distribution domain contact (mgardownload.com, m-mgarg.com) AICommand & Control High
Hunts network/DNS resolution of the two PromptSpy domains named in ESET's H1 2026 report: mgardownload[.]com (served the malicious 'MorganArg'/JPMorgan-themed dropper APK) and m-mgarg[.]com (webpage opened post-install, staging the VNC/Gemini C2 flow). Any corporate DNS resolver, proxy, or MDM-managed device touching these is a PromptSpy indicator, not a generic beacon template. Rationale: Both domains are explicitly attributed to PromptSpy by ESET's dedicated write-up (VirusTotal shows all four droppers served from mgardownload[.]com; the dropper opens m-mgarg[.]com on launch) and confirmed by The Hacker News / Cybersecurity News, so they are high-fidelity and non-generic. Dropped the AWS/Cloudflare IPs (54.67.2.84, 52.222.205.45, 104.21.91.170) as shared hosting with no second-source PromptSpy attribution. Cross-checked against: • https://www.welivesecurity.com/en/eset-research/promptspy-ushers-in-era-android-threats-using-genai/ • https://thehackernews.com/2026/02/promptspy-android-malware-abuses-google.html • https://cybersecuritynews.com/promptspy-android-ai-malware/ • https://github.com/eset/malware-ioc

Data sourcesNetwork_Resolution.DNS Web.Web
Expected false positives · estimated rate: low — model-assessed, tune to your environment

  • Passive-DNS / sinkhole collectors that log resolutions of known-bad domains
  • Security web proxy that pre-resolves URLs in blocked email for detonation
  • Managed Android (MDM/Intune) test device intentionally detonating the sample in a sandbox VLAN
Response runbook
1) Triage: identify the querying host/user and whether it is an analyst/sandbox asset or a real user endpoint; check if the resolution succeeded and whether any follow-on connection to the returned IP occurred. For Android, pull MDM inventory for a 'MorganArg'/JPMorgan-lookalike package. 2) Contain: sink-hole/block both domains at DNS and proxy; if a managed device, isolate it and initiate mobile-threat-defense scan; block the resolved IPs at egress. 3) Hunt: pivot on the resolved IPs across DeviceNetworkEvents/firewall for other internal talkers, search DeviceFileEvents/download logs for the APK sample SHA1s (see companion UC), and review any VNC-style outbound sessions from mobile subnets.

PromptSpy dropper APK sample hash landing on monitored endpoint AIDelivery Medium
Hunts the nine PromptSpy dropper APK SHA1 hashes from the ESET H1 2026 IOC bundle appearing in file telemetry — e.g. an APK downloaded to a Windows workstation/file share for sideloading, staged on a jump box, or synced from mobile backup. Exact-hash match, so any hit is the actual sample, not a lookalike. Rationale: The nine SHA1 values are the ESET-published PromptSpy dropper samples (mirrored in the eset/malware-ioc GitHub repo and VirusTotal), so an exact match is unambiguous. Detection is on file telemetry because these are Android APKs that won't execute as Windows processes — they only surface if the sample is downloaded/staged on a monitored endpoint or file share. Datadog/Falcon left empty: neither reliably carries file-write SHA1 for non-executed APKs. Cross-checked against: • https://github.com/eset/malware-ioc • https://www.welivesecurity.com/en/eset-research/promptspy-ushers-in-era-android-threats-using-genai/
ATT&CKT1105 T1204.002
Data sourcesEndpoint.Filesystem
Expected false positives · estimated rate: low — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Malware analyst deliberately downloading/storing the PromptSpy sample on a lab or research workstation
  • EDR/AV quarantine or backup copy of the sample retaining the original hash
  • Threat-intel sample-repo sync (MISP, internal malware zoo) landing files on a collector host
  • IR responder copying a captured sample to a case-evidence share
Suppression filter
| where not (FolderPath has "\\Quarantine\\" or FolderPath has "\\MalwareSamples\\" or FolderPath has "\\Evidence\\")
Response runbook
1) Triage: confirm the host role — analyst/lab/evidence host vs. a normal user endpoint; inspect FolderPath and FileOriginUrl to see whether it arrived via download (mgardownload[.]com) vs. a research tool, and identify the acquiring user/process. 2) Contain: if a production user endpoint, isolate it, delete/quarantine the APK, and check for onward transfer to any Android device via USB/MDM sideload; block the source URL. 3) Hunt: pivot the FileOriginUrl and downloading host into the companion domain-resolution UC, sweep other endpoints/file shares for the same SHA1 set, and review mobile fleet for the installed 'MorganArg'/JPMorgan-lookalike package.

Phishing-link click correlated to endpoint execution Delivery High
User received an external email containing a URL, clicked it, and within 60 seconds the recipient's endpoint spawned a scripting interpreter or network downloader (PowerShell / cmd / mshta / curl / certutil / bitsadmin). This is the high-fidelity shape — a raw "user clicked an emailed URL" query is too noisy to alert on because every Microsoft 365 tenant generates thousands of legitimate clicks per day. The exec-correlation step suppresses the noise to roughly the rate at which a click actually drives onto-host execution, which is the actionable signal. Pair with UC_PHISH_LINK_BYPASS (Safe Links override) and UC_PHISH_LINK_NEWDOMAIN for orthogonal high-fidelity variants.
ATT&CKT1566.002 T1204.001 T1059.001
Data sourcesEmail.All_Email Web Endpoint.Processes EmailEvents EmailUrlInfo UrlClickEvents DeviceProcessEvents
// Phishing-link click that drives endpoint execution within 60s.
// Far higher fidelity than "every clicked URL" — most legitimate clicks
// never spawn a non-browser child process, so the join eliminates the
// 99% of noise that makes a raw click query unactionable.
let LookbackDays = 7d;
let SuspectClicks = UrlClickEvents
    | where Timestamp > ago(LookbackDays)
    | where AccountName !endswith "$"
    | where ActionType in ("ClickAllowed","ClickedThrough")
    | join kind=inner (
        EmailEvents
        | where Timestamp > ago(LookbackDays)
        | where DeliveryAction == "Delivered"
        | where EmailDirection == "Inbound"
        | project NetworkMessageId, Subject, SenderFromAddress, SenderFromDomain,
                  RecipientEmailAddress, EmailTimestamp = Timestamp
      ) on NetworkMessageId
    | join kind=leftouter (
        EmailUrlInfo | project NetworkMessageId, Url, UrlDomain
      ) on NetworkMessageId, Url
    | project ClickTime = Timestamp, AccountUpn, IPAddress, Url, UrlDomain,
              Subject, SenderFromAddress, SenderFromDomain, RecipientEmailAddress,
              ActionType;
// Correlate to a non-browser child process spawned within 60 seconds on
// the recipient's device.
DeviceProcessEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(LookbackDays)
| where InitiatingProcessFileName in~ ("chrome.exe","msedge.exe","firefox.exe",
                                         "outlook.exe","brave.exe","arc.exe")
| where FileName in~ ("powershell.exe","pwsh.exe","cmd.exe","mshta.exe",
                        "rundll32.exe","regsvr32.exe","wscript.exe","cscript.exe",
                        "bitsadmin.exe","certutil.exe","curl.exe","wget.exe")
| join kind=inner SuspectClicks on $left.AccountName == $right.AccountUpn
| where Timestamp between (ClickTime .. ClickTime + 60s)
| project ClickTime, ProcessTime = Timestamp,
          DelaySec = datetime_diff('second', Timestamp, ClickTime),
          DeviceName, AccountName, RecipientEmailAddress, SenderFromAddress,
          Subject, Url, UrlDomain, ActionType,
          FileName, ProcessCommandLine, InitiatingProcessFileName
| order by ClickTime desc
// UrlClickEvents has no clean Sentinel-native equivalent. The detection
// pivots to: Office Send→Receive proximity to SecurityEvent 4688 of a
// non-browser child process. Lower fidelity than the Defender version.
let LookbackDays = 7d;
let SuspectMailUsers = OfficeActivity
    | where TimeGenerated > ago(LookbackDays)
    | where OfficeWorkload == "Exchange"
    | where Operation =~ "Receive"
    | summarize Subject = any(Subject), Sender = any(Sender)
                by MailboxOwnerUPN, MessageId, EmailTime = bin(TimeGenerated, 1m);
SecurityEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(LookbackDays)
| where EventID == 4688
| where ParentProcessName has_any ("\chrome.exe","\msedge.exe",
                                     "\firefox.exe","\outlook.exe","\brave.exe")
| where NewProcessName has_any ("\powershell.exe","\pwsh.exe","\cmd.exe",
                                  "\mshta.exe","\rundll32.exe","\regsvr32.exe",
                                  "\wscript.exe","\cscript.exe","\bitsadmin.exe",
                                  "\certutil.exe","\curl.exe","\wget.exe")
| join kind=inner SuspectMailUsers on $left.Account == $right.MailboxOwnerUPN
| where TimeGenerated between (EmailTime .. EmailTime + 60s)
| project TimeGenerated, EmailTime, Computer, Account, ParentProcessName,
          NewProcessName, CommandLine, Sender, Subject
| order by TimeGenerated desc
WEB
Toggle if your env has no CIM data-model acceleration.
``` Phishing-link click that drives endpoint execution within 60s ```
| tstats `summariesonly` earliest(_time) AS click_time
    from datamodel=Web
    where Web.action="allowed"
    by Web.src, Web.user, Web.dest, Web.url
| `drop_dm_object_name(Web)`
| rename user AS recipient, dest AS clicked_domain, url AS clicked_url
| join type=inner recipient
    [| tstats `summariesonly` count
         from datamodel=Email.All_Email
         where All_Email.action="delivered" AND All_Email.url!="-"
         by All_Email.recipient, All_Email.src_user, All_Email.url, All_Email.subject
     | `drop_dm_object_name(All_Email)`
     | rex field=url "https?://(?<email_domain>[^/]+)"
     | rename recipient AS recipient]
| join type=inner src
    [| tstats `summariesonly` earliest(_time) AS exec_time
         values(Processes.process) AS exec_cmd, values(Processes.process_name) AS exec_proc
         from datamodel=Endpoint.Processes
         where Processes.parent_process_name IN ("chrome.exe","msedge.exe","firefox.exe",
                                                   "outlook.exe","brave.exe","arc.exe")
           AND Processes.process_name IN ("powershell.exe","pwsh.exe","cmd.exe","mshta.exe",
                                            "rundll32.exe","regsvr32.exe","wscript.exe",
                                            "cscript.exe","bitsadmin.exe","certutil.exe",
                                            "curl.exe","wget.exe")
         by Processes.dest, Processes.user
     | `drop_dm_object_name(Processes)`
     | rename dest AS src]
| eval delta_sec = exec_time - click_time
| where delta_sec >= 0 AND delta_sec <= 60
| table click_time, exec_time, delta_sec, recipient, src, src_user, subject,
        clicked_domain, clicked_url, exec_proc, exec_cmd
| sort - click_time

Email attachment opened from external sender Delivery High
Attachment delivery + execution by recipient — most common malware initial access.
ATT&CKT1566.001 T1204.002
Data sourcesEmail.All_Email Endpoint.Processes EmailAttachmentInfo DeviceProcessEvents
let LookbackDays = 7d;
let MalAttachments = EmailAttachmentInfo
    | where Timestamp > ago(LookbackDays)
    | where AccountName !endswith "$"
    | project NetworkMessageId, RecipientEmailAddress,
              AttachmentFileName = FileName, AttachmentSHA256 = SHA256;
DeviceProcessEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(LookbackDays)
| where InitiatingProcessFileName in~ ("OUTLOOK.EXE","winword.exe","excel.exe","powerpnt.exe")
| where FileName in~ ("cmd.exe","powershell.exe","wscript.exe","cscript.exe",
                      "mshta.exe","rundll32.exe","regsvr32.exe")
| join kind=inner MalAttachments on $left.AccountUpn == $right.RecipientEmailAddress
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, AccountName, FileName, ProcessCommandLine,
          InitiatingProcessFileName, AttachmentFileName, AttachmentSHA256
// Sentinel doesn't have an attachment-hash table. Best approximation:
// OfficeActivity Send/Receive activity + correlate to host process spawn.
let LookbackDays = 7d;
let MailWithAttach = OfficeActivity
    | where TimeGenerated > ago(LookbackDays)
    | where OfficeWorkload == "Exchange"
    | where Operation in~ ("Send","Receive")
    | where isnotempty(MessageId)
    | project EmailTime = TimeGenerated, MailboxOwnerUPN, Sender,
              Recipients, Subject, MessageId;
SecurityEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(LookbackDays)
| where EventID == 4688
| where ParentProcessName endswith "OUTLOOK.EXE"
| where NewProcessName endswith "\cmd.exe"
   or NewProcessName endswith "\powershell.exe"
   or NewProcessName endswith "\wscript.exe"
   or NewProcessName endswith "\cscript.exe"
   or NewProcessName endswith "\mshta.exe"
| project TimeGenerated, Computer, Account, NewProcessName, CommandLine,
          ParentProcessName
| order by TimeGenerated desc
ENDPOINT
Toggle if your env has no CIM data-model acceleration.
| tstats `summariesonly` count
    from datamodel=Email.All_Email
    where All_Email.file_name!="-"
    by All_Email.src_user, All_Email.recipient, All_Email.file_name, All_Email.subject
| rename All_Email.recipient as user
| join type=inner user
    [| tstats `summariesonly` count
        from datamodel=Endpoint.Processes
        where Processes.parent_process_name IN ("OUTLOOK.EXE","winword.exe","excel.exe","powerpnt.exe")
          AND Processes.process_name IN ("cmd.exe","powershell.exe","wscript.exe","cscript.exe","mshta.exe","rundll32.exe","regsvr32.exe")
        by Processes.dest, Processes.user, Processes.parent_process_name, Processes.process_name, Processes.process
     | rename Processes.user as user]
| tstats summariesonly=false count
    from datamodel=Email.All_Email
    where All_Email.file_name!="-"
    by All_Email.src_user, All_Email.recipient, All_Email.file_name, All_Email.subject
| rename All_Email.recipient as user
| join type=inner user
    [| tstats summariesonly=false count
        from datamodel=Endpoint.Processes
        where Processes.parent_process_name IN ("OUTLOOK.EXE","winword.exe","excel.exe","powerpnt.exe")
          AND Processes.process_name IN ("cmd.exe","powershell.exe","wscript.exe","cscript.exe","mshta.exe","rundll32.exe","regsvr32.exe")
        by Processes.dest, Processes.user, Processes.parent_process_name, Processes.process_name, Processes.process
     | rename Processes.user as user]

title: FakeCaptcha / ClickFix - Clipboard-Injected PowerShell from Explorer

status: experimental
description: |
    "FakeCaptcha" / "ClickFix" social-engineering: malicious site asks
    user to press Win+R and paste a payload. The result is
    powershell/mshta launched directly from explorer.exe with iex /
    base64 / downloadstring in the command line.
references:
    - https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1059/001/
    - https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1204/002/
author: Clankerusecase
date: 2026/05/02
tags:
    - attack.t1059.001
    - attack.t1204.002
    - attack.execution
logsource:
    category: process_creation
    product: windows
detection:
    selection_parent:
        ParentImage|endswith:
            - '\explorer.exe'
            - '\RuntimeBroker.exe'
    selection_child:
        Image|endswith:
            - '\powershell.exe'
            - '\pwsh.exe'
            - '\mshta.exe'
    selection_cmd:
        CommandLine|contains:
            - 'iex'
            - 'invoke-expression'
            - 'frombase64'
            - 'downloadstring'
            - 'hxxp'
            - 'curl '
            - 'wget '
    condition: selection_parent and selection_child and selection_cmd
falsepositives:
    - IT-driven scripted automation that admins paste-launch
level: high
ENDPOINT
Toggle if your env has no CIM data-model acceleration.
| tstats `summariesonly` count min(_time) as firstTime max(_time) as lastTime
    from datamodel=Endpoint.Processes
    where Processes.parent_process_name IN ("explorer.exe","RuntimeBroker.exe")
      AND Processes.process_name IN ("powershell.exe","pwsh.exe","mshta.exe")
      AND (Processes.process="*iex*" OR Processes.process="*Invoke-Expression*"
        OR Processes.process="*FromBase64*" OR Processes.process="*DownloadString*"
        OR Processes.process="*hxxp*" OR Processes.process="*curl*" OR Processes.process="*wget*")
    by Processes.dest, Processes.user, Processes.process, Processes.parent_process_name
| `drop_dm_object_name(Processes)`
| tstats summariesonly=false count min(_time) as firstTime max(_time) as lastTime
    from datamodel=Endpoint.Processes
    where Processes.parent_process_name IN ("explorer.exe","RuntimeBroker.exe")
      AND Processes.process_name IN ("powershell.exe","pwsh.exe","mshta.exe")
      AND (Processes.process="*iex*" OR Processes.process="*Invoke-Expression*"
        OR Processes.process="*FromBase64*" OR Processes.process="*DownloadString*"
        OR Processes.process="*hxxp*" OR Processes.process="*curl*" OR Processes.process="*wget*")
    by Processes.dest, Processes.user, Processes.process, Processes.parent_process_name
| `drop_dm_object_name(Processes)`
Ransomware-style mass file rename / extension change Actions on Objectives Medium
Threshold detection: many files renamed in short window, often with new extension.
ATT&CKT1486
Data sourcesEndpoint.Filesystem DeviceFileEvents
DeviceFileEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(1d)
| where InitiatingProcessAccountName !endswith "$"
| where ActionType in ("FileRenamed","FileModified")
| summarize files = dcount(FileName) by DeviceName, InitiatingProcessAccountName, bin(Timestamp, 1m)
| where files > 200    // empirical: > 200 unique-file renames in 1m by one account on one host
                       //            is well above the P99 of legitimate bulk-tooling
| order by files desc

ImFileEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(1d)
| where ActorUsername !endswith "$"
| where EventType in ("FileRenamed","FileModified")
| summarize files = dcount(TargetFileName)
            by DvcHostname, ActorUsername, ActingProcessName, bin(TimeGenerated, 1m)
| where files > 200    // P99 of legit bulk-tooling per-minute rename volume
| order by files desc
ENDPOINT
Toggle if your env has no CIM data-model acceleration.
| tstats `summariesonly` count, dc(Filesystem.file_name) AS files
    from datamodel=Endpoint.Filesystem
    where Filesystem.action IN ("modified","renamed")
    by Filesystem.dest, Filesystem.user, _time span=1m
| `drop_dm_object_name(Filesystem)`
| where files > 200
| sort - files
| tstats summariesonly=false count, dc(Filesystem.file_name) AS files
    from datamodel=Endpoint.Filesystem
    where Filesystem.action IN ("modified","renamed")
    by Filesystem.dest, Filesystem.user, _time span=1m
| `drop_dm_object_name(Filesystem)`
| where files > 200
| sort - files
LSASS process access / dump (credential theft) Actions on Objectives High
Mimikatz, comsvcs.dll MiniDump, or any non-Windows process opening LSASS.
ATT&CKT1003.001 T1003
Data sourcesEndpoint.Processes DeviceEvents
DeviceEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(7d)
| where AccountName !endswith "$"
| where ActionType == "OpenProcessApiCall"
| where FileName =~ "lsass.exe"
| where InitiatingProcessFileName !in~ ("MsSense.exe","MsMpEng.exe","csrss.exe",
                                          "svchost.exe","wininit.exe","services.exe",
                                          "lsm.exe","SearchProtocolHost.exe")
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, ActionType, FileName,
          InitiatingProcessFileName, InitiatingProcessCommandLine,
          InitiatingProcessFolderPath, AccountName
| order by Timestamp desc
// SecurityEvent EventID 4663 = object access. AccessMask 0x10 / 0x40 / 0x1010
// indicate read access to lsass.exe — credential-dump signature. Audit
// Object Access > Audit File System policy required.
SecurityEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(7d)
| where EventID == 4663
| where ObjectName endswith "\lsass.exe"
| where Account !endswith "$"
| project TimeGenerated, Computer, Account, ObjectName, ProcessName,
          AccessMask, AccessReason
| order by TimeGenerated desc

File hash IOCs — endpoint file/process match Installation High
Match SHA256/SHA1/MD5 named in the article against EDR file/process telemetry.
ATT&CKT1027
Data sourcesEndpoint.Filesystem Endpoint.Processes DeviceFileEvents DeviceProcessEvents
// Pre-filter each table BEFORE the union — the engine cannot push
// predicates across `union`, and DeviceFileEvents lacks ProcessCommandLine
// (Initiating only) so column-projection has to differ per side.
union
    ( DeviceFileEvents
        | where Timestamp > ago(7d)
        | where InitiatingProcessAccountName !endswith "$"
        | where SHA256 in~ ("6bbc9ab132ba066f63676e05da13d108598bc29b", "375d7423e63c8f5f2cc814e8cfe697ba25168afa", "3978ac5cd14e357320e127d6c87f10cb70a1dcc2", "e60d12017d2da579df87368f5596a0244621ae86", "9b1723284e311794987997cb7e8814eb6014713f", "076801bd9c6eb78fc0331a4c7a22c73199cc3824", "8364730e9bb2cf3a4b016de1b34f38341c0ee2fa", "f8f4c5bc498bcce907dc975dd88be8d594629909", "c14e9b062ed28115ede096788f62b47a6ed841ac") or SHA1 in~ ("6bbc9ab132ba066f63676e05da13d108598bc29b", "375d7423e63c8f5f2cc814e8cfe697ba25168afa", "3978ac5cd14e357320e127d6c87f10cb70a1dcc2", "e60d12017d2da579df87368f5596a0244621ae86", "9b1723284e311794987997cb7e8814eb6014713f", "076801bd9c6eb78fc0331a4c7a22c73199cc3824", "8364730e9bb2cf3a4b016de1b34f38341c0ee2fa", "f8f4c5bc498bcce907dc975dd88be8d594629909", "c14e9b062ed28115ede096788f62b47a6ed841ac") or MD5 in~ ("6bbc9ab132ba066f63676e05da13d108598bc29b", "375d7423e63c8f5f2cc814e8cfe697ba25168afa", "3978ac5cd14e357320e127d6c87f10cb70a1dcc2", "e60d12017d2da579df87368f5596a0244621ae86", "9b1723284e311794987997cb7e8814eb6014713f", "076801bd9c6eb78fc0331a4c7a22c73199cc3824", "8364730e9bb2cf3a4b016de1b34f38341c0ee2fa", "f8f4c5bc498bcce907dc975dd88be8d594629909", "c14e9b062ed28115ede096788f62b47a6ed841ac")
        | project Timestamp, DeviceName, ActionType, FileName, FolderPath, SHA256,
                  Cmd = InitiatingProcessCommandLine, Source = "DeviceFileEvents" ),
    ( DeviceProcessEvents
        | where Timestamp > ago(7d)
        | where AccountName !endswith "$"
        | where SHA256 in~ ("6bbc9ab132ba066f63676e05da13d108598bc29b", "375d7423e63c8f5f2cc814e8cfe697ba25168afa", "3978ac5cd14e357320e127d6c87f10cb70a1dcc2", "e60d12017d2da579df87368f5596a0244621ae86", "9b1723284e311794987997cb7e8814eb6014713f", "076801bd9c6eb78fc0331a4c7a22c73199cc3824", "8364730e9bb2cf3a4b016de1b34f38341c0ee2fa", "f8f4c5bc498bcce907dc975dd88be8d594629909", "c14e9b062ed28115ede096788f62b47a6ed841ac") or SHA1 in~ ("6bbc9ab132ba066f63676e05da13d108598bc29b", "375d7423e63c8f5f2cc814e8cfe697ba25168afa", "3978ac5cd14e357320e127d6c87f10cb70a1dcc2", "e60d12017d2da579df87368f5596a0244621ae86", "9b1723284e311794987997cb7e8814eb6014713f", "076801bd9c6eb78fc0331a4c7a22c73199cc3824", "8364730e9bb2cf3a4b016de1b34f38341c0ee2fa", "f8f4c5bc498bcce907dc975dd88be8d594629909", "c14e9b062ed28115ede096788f62b47a6ed841ac") or MD5 in~ ("6bbc9ab132ba066f63676e05da13d108598bc29b", "375d7423e63c8f5f2cc814e8cfe697ba25168afa", "3978ac5cd14e357320e127d6c87f10cb70a1dcc2", "e60d12017d2da579df87368f5596a0244621ae86", "9b1723284e311794987997cb7e8814eb6014713f", "076801bd9c6eb78fc0331a4c7a22c73199cc3824", "8364730e9bb2cf3a4b016de1b34f38341c0ee2fa", "f8f4c5bc498bcce907dc975dd88be8d594629909", "c14e9b062ed28115ede096788f62b47a6ed841ac")
        | project Timestamp, DeviceName, ActionType, FileName, FolderPath, SHA256,
                  Cmd = ProcessCommandLine, Source = "DeviceProcessEvents" )
| order by Timestamp desc

// Pre-filter both ASIM tables before the union — same pattern as the
// Defender version so the engine can push hash predicates per-side.
let BadHashes = dynamic(["6bbc9ab132ba066f63676e05da13d108598bc29b", "375d7423e63c8f5f2cc814e8cfe697ba25168afa", "3978ac5cd14e357320e127d6c87f10cb70a1dcc2", "e60d12017d2da579df87368f5596a0244621ae86", "9b1723284e311794987997cb7e8814eb6014713f", "076801bd9c6eb78fc0331a4c7a22c73199cc3824", "8364730e9bb2cf3a4b016de1b34f38341c0ee2fa", "f8f4c5bc498bcce907dc975dd88be8d594629909", "c14e9b062ed28115ede096788f62b47a6ed841ac"]);
union
    ( ImFileEvent
        | where TimeGenerated > ago(7d)
        | where ActorUsername !endswith "$"
        | where TargetFileSHA256 in~ (BadHashes)
           or TargetFileSHA1 in~ (BadHashes)
           or TargetFileMD5 in~ (BadHashes)
        | project TimeGenerated, DvcHostname, EventType,
                  TargetFileName, TargetFilePath, TargetFileSHA256,
                  Cmd = ActingProcessName, Source = "ImFileEvent" ),
    ( ImProcessCreate
        | where TimeGenerated > ago(7d)
        | where ActorUsername !endswith "$"
        | where SHA256 in~ (BadHashes) or SHA1 in~ (BadHashes) or MD5 in~ (BadHashes)
        | project TimeGenerated, DvcHostname, EventType = TargetProcessName,
                  TargetFileName = TargetProcessName, TargetFilePath = TargetProcessName,
                  TargetFileSHA256 = SHA256,
                  Cmd = TargetProcessCommandLine, Source = "ImProcessCreate" )
| order by TimeGenerated desc

title: File or Process Matching Article Hash IOCs

description: |

Data sourcesVulnerabilities DeviceInfo DeviceTvmSoftwareVulnerabilities
// TVM tables are daily snapshots — pin a 1-day window so the engine
// partitions on Timestamp instead of scanning the full retention.
DeviceTvmSoftwareVulnerabilities
| where Timestamp > ago(1d)
| where CveId in~ ("CVE-2026-48908")
| join kind=inner (DeviceInfo | where Timestamp > ago(1d)) on DeviceId
| project DeviceName, OSPlatform, CveId, VulnerabilitySeverityLevel, RecommendedSecurityUpdate
| order by VulnerabilitySeverityLevel asc, DeviceName asc

// Sentinel has no native TVM table. If MDE→Sentinel streaming is enabled,
// `DeviceTvmSoftwareVulnerabilities` is available. Otherwise this UC has
// no Sentinel translation — track via Update / Heartbeat OS-version
// gaps as a coarse approximation.
DeviceTvmSoftwareVulnerabilities
| where TimeGenerated > ago(1d)
| where CveId in~ ("CVE-2026-48908")
| join kind=inner (DeviceInfo | where TimeGenerated > ago(1d)) on DeviceId
| project DeviceName, OSPlatform, CveId,
          VulnerabilitySeverityLevel, RecommendedSecurityUpdate
| order by VulnerabilitySeverityLevel asc, DeviceName asc

Rocket.Chat Livechat file-upload ID enumeration sweep (ObjectId harvest) AIActions on Objectives High
Hunts an unauthenticated source pulling many distinct /file-upload/{fileId} objects while carrying the Livechat authorization params (rc_room_type=l + rc_token) — the continuous ObjectId-prediction harvest described in the Aikido disclosure. High volume of distinct fileIds from one IP via the Livechat auth path is the signature of the mass file-capture exploit. Rationale: Anchors on the exact exploit request shape from the article's Python PoC — GET /file-upload/{fileId} with rc_room_type=l and rc_token query params — combined with a distinct-fileId volume threshold that captures the 'retrieve all generated valid IDs continuously' harvest. Legit Livechat file access does not fan out across dozens of unrelated fileIds. Cross-checked against: • https://www.aikido.dev/blog/predicting-mongodb-objectid-rocket-chat • https://hackerone.com/reports/3687142 • https://docs.rocket.chat/docs/rocketchat-security-fixes-updates-and-advisories • https://github.com/RocketChat/Rocket.Chat/releases/tag/8.5.0
ATT&CKT1213 T1190
Data sourcesWeb.Web
Expected false positives · estimated rate: low — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • A genuinely busy Livechat helpdesk session where a visitor downloads many attachments the agent sent (all belonging to that room)
  • Load balancer / uptime monitor health-checking a file-upload URL repeatedly (usually one fixed path, not distinct fileIds)
  • Internal backup or migration tooling iterating over uploads with a service token
  • Authorized DAST/vulnerability scanner (Aikido, Burp) replaying the PoC against a staging instance
  • CDN origin prefetch pulling attachments
Suppression filter
| where UserAgents !has_any ("kube-probe","ELB-HealthChecker","UptimeRobot","Pingdom")
Response runbook
1) Triage: pull the source IP's full request timeline; confirm the requests carry rc_room_type=l + rc_token and hit many DISTINCT fileIds, and check whether the Rocket.Chat build predates 8.5.1/8.4.4/8.3.6/8.2.6/8.1.6/8.0.7/7.13.9/7.10.13 (vulnerable). 2) Contain: block the source IP at the WAF/reverse proxy, and if patch is not yet deployed, disable Livechat (Admin > Omnichannel) or upgrade immediately. 3) Hunt: enumerate which fileIds returned HTTP 200 to that IP to scope leaked files, and search for the same IP creating anonymous visitors (POST /api/v1/livechat/visitor) to identify the session token used.
ImWebSession
| where TimeGenerated > ago(1h)
| where Url has "/file-upload/" and (Url has "rc_room_type=l" or Url has "rc_token=")
| extend FileId = extract(@"/file-upload/([^/?]+)", 1, Url)
| where isnotempty(FileId)
| summarize DistinctFiles = dcount(FileId), Requests = count(), FirstSeen = min(TimeGenerated), LastSeen = max(TimeGenerated), UserAgents = make_set(HttpRequestHeaderUserAgent, 5), Statuses = make_set(HttpStatusCode, 10) by SrcIpAddr, DstHostname
| where DistinctFiles >= 25   // >=25 distinct file-upload IDs fetched via the Livechat auth path from one source in 1h = ObjectId harvest sweep
| order by DistinctFiles desc

| tstats `summariesonly` count as total_requests dc(Web.uri_path) as distinct_files min(_time) as firstTime max(_time) as lastTime values(Web.status) as statuses values(Web.http_user_agent) as user_agent from datamodel=Web where Web.uri_path="/file-upload/*" (Web.uri_query="*rc_room_type=l*" OR Web.uri_query="*rc_token=*") by Web.src Web.dest
| `drop_dm_object_name(Web)`
| where distinct_files >= 25

Rocket.Chat anonymous Livechat visitor bootstrap chained to file-upload access AIExploitation Medium
Detects the full unauthenticated exploit chain: a single source registering an anonymous Livechat visitor (POST /api/v1/livechat/visitor), requesting a room (GET /api/v1/livechat/room), then reading files via /file-upload/ within a short window. This is the session-bootstrap primitive the exploit uses to mint a valid rc_token/rc_rid before harvesting arbitrary files. Rationale: Chains the three exact endpoints from the PoC (POST /api/v1/livechat/visitor, GET /api/v1/livechat/room, GET /file-upload/) within a 10-minute window keyed on source IP — the minimum footprint of the unauthenticated access-control bypass. Individually noisy, together it is the exploit workflow. Cross-checked against: • https://www.aikido.dev/blog/predicting-mongodb-objectid-rocket-chat • https://hackerone.com/reports/3687142 • https://github.com/RocketChat/Rocket.Chat/releases/tag/8.5.0
ATT&CKT1190 T1213
Data sourcesWeb.Web
Expected false positives · estimated rate: medium — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • A real anonymous helpdesk visitor who opens Livechat and then downloads a file the agent shared (legitimate, same room)
  • Synthetic monitoring that scripts a Livechat conversation end-to-end
  • Support-widget embedded on a high-traffic page generating many short-lived visitor sessions
  • Rocket.Chat mobile/desktop client polling room + upload endpoints during normal use
  • Pen-test / bug-bounty researcher reproducing the chain on an authorized instance
Response runbook
1) Triage: confirm the visitor registration and file reads share one SrcIpAddr and that the /file-upload/ requests carry rc_room_type=l; verify the instance version against the patched list. 2) Contain: block the IP at the proxy/WAF and, if unpatched, disable Livechat or upgrade to the fixed build. 3) Hunt: pivot on the source IP to the enumeration-sweep detection to measure how many files were pulled, and review Content-Disposition/response sizes to identify sensitive filenames leaked.
ImWebSession
| where TimeGenerated > ago(1h)
| where Url has_any ("/api/v1/livechat/visitor", "/api/v1/livechat/room", "/file-upload/")
| extend isVisitor = Url has "/api/v1/livechat/visitor", isRoom = Url has "/api/v1/livechat/room", isFile = Url has "/file-upload/"
| summarize VisitorReg = countif(isVisitor), RoomReq = countif(isRoom), FileReq = countif(isFile), FirstSeen = min(TimeGenerated), LastSeen = max(TimeGenerated) by SrcIpAddr, DstHostname, bin(TimeGenerated, 10m)
| where VisitorReg >= 1 and RoomReq >= 1 and FileReq >= 1   // same source bootstraps an anon visitor+room then reads uploads within 10m
| order by FileReq desc

| `drop_dm_object_name(Web)`
| eval isVisitor=if(uri_path="/api/v1/livechat/visitor",1,0), isRoom=if(uri_path="/api/v1/livechat/room",1,0), isFile=if(like(uri_path,"/file-upload/%"),1,0)
| stats sum(isVisitor) as visitorReg sum(isRoom) as roomReq sum(isFile) as fileReq dc(uri_path) as distinctPaths min(_time) as firstTime max(_time) as lastTime by src dest
| where visitorReg>=1 AND roomReq>=1 AND fileReq>=1

| sort - fileReq

| stats sum(isVisitor) as visitorReg sum(isRoom) as roomReq sum(isFile) as fileReq dc(uri_path) as distinctPaths min(_time) as firstTime max(_time) as lastTime by src dest

Rocket.Chat file-upload request carrying Livechat auth params (IDOR signature) AIExploitation Medium
Single-event signature for the Rocket.Chat access-control bypass: a GET to /file-upload/ whose query string carries rc_room_type=l together with rc_token — the Livechat authorization path being used to read a file, exactly as in the disclosed exploit. Surfaces individual exploit attempts even below the harvest threshold. Rationale: Uses the verbatim exploit primitive from the PoC — /file-upload/ path plus rc_room_type=l and rc_token query params — as an atomic, Sigma-portable signature. It matches even a single probe, complementing the volume- and chain-based UCs. Cross-checked against: • https://www.aikido.dev/blog/predicting-mongodb-objectid-rocket-chat • https://hackerone.com/reports/3687142
ATT&CKT1190
Data sourcesWeb.Web
Expected false positives · estimated rate: medium — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Legitimate Livechat visitor downloading an attachment shared in their own helpdesk room (identical request shape)
  • Rocket.Chat client appending rc_room_type/rc_token to file URLs during normal Livechat file rendering
  • WAF or SSL-inspection proxy replaying the request as part of active response testing
  • Authorized researcher/DAST scan on a staging instance
  • URL-preview/link-unfurl bot following a Livechat file link
Response runbook
1) Triage: check the response status — HTTP 200 means a file was served; note the SrcIpAddr, Content-Disposition filename, and whether the source ever authenticated. 2) Contain: if the instance is unpatched (pre 8.5.1/8.4.4/8.3.6/8.2.6/8.1.6/8.0.7/7.13.9/7.10.13), upgrade or disable Livechat and block the IP. 3) Hunt: aggregate this IP's requests to see if it escalates into the distinct-fileId harvest sweep, and correlate with anonymous visitor registrations from the same address.
ImWebSession
| where TimeGenerated > ago(24h)
| where HttpMethod =~ "GET"
| where Url has "/file-upload/" and Url has "rc_room_type=l" and Url has "rc_token="
| project TimeGenerated, SrcIpAddr, DstHostname, HttpMethod, Url, HttpStatusCode, HttpRequestHeaderUserAgent
| order by TimeGenerated desc

phpBB CVE-2026-48611 auth bypass via login_link auth_provider=apache AIExploitation High
Hunts the exact CVE-2026-48611 exploit request: a single unauthenticated POST to ucp.php that triggers the login-link flow but forces the vulnerable 'apache' auth provider (auth_provider=apache) to skip the password check and log in as any user. The auth_provider=apache value inside a mode=login_link request is a near-unambiguous exploit signature that no legitimate default phpBB flow produces. Rationale: Anchored on the article's verbatim PoC URL (/ucp.php?mode=login_link&auth_provider=apache&login_link_aikido=1); auth_provider=apache in a login_link request is the exact exploit primitive and has no benign default-config equivalent. Cross-checked against Pentest-Tools, IONIX, SentinelOne, phpBB.com advisory and public PoC repos. Cross-checked against: • https://pentest-tools.com/research/phpbb-authentication-bypass • https://www.ionix.io/threat-center/cve-2026-48611/ • https://www.sentinelone.com/vulnerability-database/cve-2026-48611/ • https://www.bleepingcomputer.com/news/security/phpbb-forum-fixes-auth-bypass-bug-lurking-for-a-decade/ • https://www.phpbb.com/community/viewtopic.php?t=2672170
ATT&CKT1190 T1078
Data sourcesWeb
Expected false positives · estimated rate: low — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Authorized vulnerability scanning (Nuclei has a public CVE-2026-48611 template) hitting the endpoint
  • Internal penetration-test / red-team validation of the patch
  • A phpBB instance legitimately fronted by an Apache .htpasswd proxy that genuinely uses the apache auth provider (rare, non-default)
  • Security researchers reproducing the PoC from the aikido.dev / GitHub repos against a lab instance
Suppression filter
| where SrcIpAddr !in ("<scanner-ip-allowlist>")
Response runbook
1) Triage: confirm the target forum version — if < 3.3.17 (or 4.0.0-a2) it is exploitable; capture source IP, User-Agent, targeted login_username, and the HTTP status (302 = successful bypass). 2) Contain: block the source IP at the WAF, force-expire all active phpBB sessions (rotate the board's session salt / clear phpbb_sessions), and prioritise upgrade to 3.3.17 or apply the vendor workaround disabling the apache provider. 3) Hunt: pivot on the same source IP for follow-on /adm/index.php access, ACP user/permission changes, and private-message reads; review phpbb_log for admin actions after the exploit timestamp.
ImWebSession
| where TimeGenerated > ago(7d)
| where Url has "ucp.php"
| where Url has "mode=login_link" and Url has "auth_provider=apache"
| project TimeGenerated, SrcIpAddr, DstHostname, HttpMethod, Url, HttpStatusCode, HttpRequestHeaderUserAgent
| order by TimeGenerated desc

phpBB CVE-2026-48611 post-exploit ACP access from exploiting IP AIActions on Objectives High
Correlates the CVE-2026-48611 exploit request (login_link + auth_provider=apache) with a subsequent hit to the phpBB Admin Control Panel (/adm/index.php) from the same source IP within one hour. This confirms the bypass yielded an admin session and the attacker is now operating the forum backend, separating real compromise from opportunistic scanning. Rationale: Uses the article's ACP path (/adm/index.php) plus the exact exploit query string, tied on source IP within a 1h window (3600s / 1h) — the exploit-then-admin sequence is what turns a scan into confirmed admin takeover. ACP path and admin impact confirmed against phpBB.com advisory and BleepingComputer. Cross-checked against: • https://www.bleepingcomputer.com/news/security/phpbb-forum-fixes-auth-bypass-bug-lurking-for-a-decade/ • https://www.phpbb.com/community/viewtopic.php?t=2672170 • https://pentest-tools.com/research/phpbb-authentication-bypass
ATT&CKT1078 T1190
Data sourcesWeb
Expected false positives · estimated rate: low — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • A legitimate admin who happens to share a NAT/egress IP with a scanner that probed the endpoint
  • Penetration test that both exploits and logs into ACP from the same host (expected TP but authorized)
  • WAF/proxy that rewrites source IP to a single upstream address, collapsing distinct users onto one src (tune to use X-Forwarded-For)
  • Load-balancer health checks hitting /adm/index.php returning 401/403 (filter on HttpStatusCode success)
Suppression filter
| where HttpStatusCode in (200, 302, 301)
Response runbook
1) Triage: confirm both events share the true client IP (check XFF if behind a proxy) and that the /adm access returned 200/302 rather than 401/403; identify which admin username was impersonated. 2) Contain: invalidate all sessions, disable/rotate the compromised admin account credentials, block the source IP, and enable maintenance mode until 3.3.17 is deployed. 3) Hunt: enumerate every ACP action from that session — new admin/mod accounts (acp_users, acp_groups), permission grants, board settings and email-config changes, and extension installs (potential webshell); diff phpbb_config and phpbb_users against a known-good backup.

| extend DelaySec = datetime_diff('second', TimeGenerated, ExploitTime)

| order by ExploitTime desc

HTTP Basic Authorization header sent to phpBB login_link endpoint AIExploitation Medium
Hunts the mechanism CVE-2026-48611 abuses: an HTTP 'Authorization: Basic' header supplied to phpBB's ucp.php login_link flow, which the apache provider trusts as PHP_AUTH_USER to skip password validation. Default phpBB never uses HTTP Basic authentication, so a Basic header on a login_link request is a strong exploit indicator that survives WAF logs even when query strings are truncated or the provider value varies. Rationale: Anchored on the PoC's 'Authorization: Basic YWRtaW46eA==' header combined with mode=login_link on ucp.php — the apache provider reads PHP_AUTH_USER from exactly this header. Basic auth on phpBB is anomalous by design; the Splunk fallback keys on the login_link POST since CIM Web has no request-header field (the header check requires ImWebSession/WAF telemetry, noted for the analyst). Cross-checked against: • https://www.aikido.dev/blog/authentication-bypass-phpbb-technical-writeup • https://pentest-tools.com/research/phpbb-authentication-bypass • https://www.ionix.io/threat-center/cve-2026-48611/
ATT&CKT1190 T1078
Data sourcesWeb
Expected false positives · estimated rate: low — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • A phpBB instance genuinely deployed behind an Apache .htpasswd proxy using the apache auth provider (non-default, legitimate Basic auth)
  • Automated vulnerability scanners replaying the PoC request
  • Browser/basic-auth prompts on a reverse proxy protecting the whole forum with site-wide Basic auth
  • API clients or monitoring tools mistakenly configured to send Basic credentials to ucp.php
Suppression filter
| where HttpStatusCode in (200, 302)
Response runbook
1) Triage: base64-decode the Authorization header to recover the targeted username and check whether the response was a 302 (successful bypass); confirm the forum is not intentionally behind an Apache .htpasswd proxy. 2) Contain: block the source IP, expire active sessions, and fast-track the 3.3.17 upgrade or apply the vendor workaround disabling the apache provider. 3) Hunt: correlate the same IP/username to subsequent /adm/index.php access, private-message reads, and ACP configuration or account changes; review other endpoints for reuse of the same Basic header.
ImWebSession
| where TimeGenerated > ago(7d)
| where Url has "ucp.php" and Url has "mode=login_link"
| where isnotempty(HttpRequestHeaderAuthorization) and HttpRequestHeaderAuthorization startswith "Basic "
| project TimeGenerated, SrcIpAddr, DstHostname, HttpMethod, Url, HttpStatusCode, HttpRequestHeaderAuthorization, HttpRequestHeaderUserAgent
| order by TimeGenerated desc
